# Chapter 1 Reconceptualizing Web3 as a human-centered infrastructure for the digital economy in the age of AI: An Information Theory and Political Economy approach

1.  Andrzej Gwizdalski
2.  University of Western Australia, Crawley, WA, Australia

## Abstract

This chapter proposes a comprehensive and interdisciplinary framework for reconceptualizing Web3 as a human-centric information communication infrastructure for the digital economy. This approach moves beyond the inconsistent web versioning models currently in use. By drawing on Information Theory, this chapter defines Web3 as a decentralized, “phygital” Internet infrastructure that enables peer-to-peer communication, governance, and the creation and ownership of digital assets. Additionally, by applying political economic theory, Web3 is contextualized within the historical evolution of the Internet through three phases of control by key stakeholders: the state, corporations, and the people, who are the core of Web3. From this perspective, Web3 is positioned as a new means of production for the digital age, facilitating direct peer-to-peer value creation and exchange in the 21st-century economy. This offers the potential for a more inclusive, stakeholder-driven capitalism and an advanced form of direct democracy. Importantly, as AI continues to evolve, Web3 may represent humanity's best hope for maintaining control and fostering a more equitable digital future.

## Keywords

Web3

Information Theory

##  1 Introduction

In this chapter, Web3 is positioned as a transformative physical and digital (hereafter “phygital”) infrastructure, facilitating direct, peer-to-peer (P2P) communication of information and creation, ownership, and transfer of value. However, the concept of Web3 has, in many cases, been diluted by rebranding efforts from Web2 incumbents and confused with the inconsistent versioning of the World Wide Web (WWW) in the literature \[1\]. This chapter seeks to provide a comprehensive and interdisciplinary framework for reconceptualizing Web3 by moving beyond these inconsistencies and defining its role as a human-centered infrastructure for the digital economy.

In recent years, Web3 somehow became a buzzword vaguely used by both disruptors and incumbents to describe their innovations.^([¹](#fn1))

This chapter attempts to provide that framework. While it does not claim to offer the only valid interpretation of Web3, it aims to shed new light on the concept and explore its broader implications through an interdisciplinary lens. The approach is informed by the author's extensive background, which spans over two decades of academic research and industry practice in fields such as Information Theory, Communication Science, Anthropology and Sociology, Digital Economy and Finance, Blockchain Technologies and Foundational Knowledge, Artificial Intelligence (AI), and Quantum Computing.

The chapter begins by reviewing current concepts and frameworks related to Web3, highlighting inconsistencies and gaps in the literature. Following this, it expands on the history of the Internet, tracing its origins back to the mid-20th century through the lens of Information Theory and Political Economy. This historical context allows for a clearer understanding of Web3’s place within the broader Internet evolution. By considering Web3 through the lens of Information Theory, the chapter argues that Web3 represents a decentralized infrastructure that enables direct P2P communication of information, which further encourages decentralized governance and the creation and ownership of digital assets. This decentralized infrastructure is what distinguishes Web3 from previous iterations of the Internet.

Furthermore, this chapter incorporates the political economy of communication to examine how the ownership of Web3’s decentralized infrastructure could redistribute power in the digital economy. Historically, control over the Internet's infrastructure has rested with either the state or corporate entities. Web3, however, shifts control to individual users, offering the potential for a more inclusive and democratic digital economy. This is also a nod to its human-centered focus in the age of AI. Taking into account new emerging technologies, such as AI and quantum computing, this chapter presents them as part of the Web3 Tech Stack and contrasts the decentralized Web3 technologies with the centralized Internet architecture for clarity. Importantly, the rpresented technologies are seen only as tools supporting the overall objectives of Web3.

This chapter concludes by situating Web3 as a new means of production for the digital age—enabling direct P2P value creation and exchange, with the potential to foster a more equitable and sustainable stakeholder-driven capitalism. In doing so, Web3 offers an advanced form of direct democracy. As AI continues to evolve, Web3’s decentralized infrastructure may also represent humanity's best hope for safeguarding personal autonomy and preventing the monopolization of powerful technologies.

##  2 Web3 literature review

This section reviews purposefully selected works that define the emerging concept of Web3 in recent years. The objective is to identify key common features of Web3 and areas of inconsistencies in research. These will then be subject to further analysis and discussion in the following sections of this chapter, to arrive at a coherent conceptual framework for defining the Web3.

###  2.1 Research process and sample selection

The purpose of this meta-review is to synthesize the most relevant and influential works on Web3, highlighting key features, technologies, and inconsistencies within existing literature. To achieve this, an organized process was undertaken to identify and refine the research sample.

The first step involved conducting an extensive search using key terms such as “Web3,” “definition,” “concept,” and “review.” This search was conducted across various academic databases, such as Google Scholar, alongside popular global search trends over the last 10 years. Google Trends data was particularly useful in identifying the timeframe during which Web3 gained broader public interest, with a noticeable surge occurring around 2021. Popular terms associated with this surge included “Non-Fungible Tokens (NFT),” “Metaverse,” and “Metamask,” with countries such as China, Nigeria, Hong Kong, and Singapore leading global interest.

This initial search resulted in over 700 potential sources, spanning a range of publications and disciplines. To ensure a manageable and relevant sample size, several criteria were established for narrowing the pool of literature.

Sample refinement: The process of refinement involved purposefully filtering studies based on:

*   • Relevance: Sources that directly addressed the definition, key features, or technological underpinnings of Web3 were prioritized.
*   • Timeframe: Given the rapid pace of Web3 developments, only works published after 2021 were considered for the final review, except for those with seminal historical significance.
*   • Perspective: Sources were selected from a variety of perspectives—technological, historical, economic, and cultural—to ensure a well-rounded view of Web3 and its implications.
*   • Academic rigor: Peer-reviewed journal articles and book chapters that focused on reviewing Web3 sources were given preference to maintain credibility, though influential thought leadership pieces were included where necessary (e.g., \[2\]).

From the initial pool, this process of filtering reduced the sample to approximately 20 works, which were further refined to less than 10 core sources when recognizing data saturation in repetitive definitions of Web3. These final sources were chosen for their diverse perspectives on Web3, including:

*   • Technological perspectives \[3–5\]
*   • Historical evolution of the Internet \[6,7\]
*   • Ecosystem-based analysis \[8\]
*   • Theoretical, economic, and cultural dimensions (Tapscott, 2023) \[1\]

###  2.2 Rationale for selection

The selected sources represent a range of scholarly and professional expertise, allowing for a comprehensive review of Web3. Technological perspectives were chosen to clarify Web3’s foundational architecture and tools, while historical studies provided context on how Web3 fits within the broader evolution of the Internet. Theoretical and cultural works were crucial in framing Web3 as not just a technical shift but a socio-political one that could transform economic systems.

However, it is important to acknowledge certain limitations in this review. While the meta-review synthesizes a broad spectrum of viewpoints, it inevitably excludes some specific aspects of Web3 due to constraints on sample size. Additionally, the rapidly evolving nature of Web3 technologies means that some sources may become outdated as new developments emerge. Nonetheless, the sources included in this review represent the most current and influential discussions on Web3 to date.

###  2.3 Findings

The findings from the literature survey focus on presenting two outcomes desired for conceptualizing Web3. The first part focuses on common core features and technologies characterizing Web3, and the second part addresses inconsistencies in research when conceptualizing Web3.

####  2.3.1 Core features of Web3

Across the reviewed literature, certain core features of Web3 were consistently identified. These features are seen as the defining characteristics of the decentralized web and differentiate Web3 from its predecessors:

*   • Decentralization: All sources unanimously agree that decentralization is the most fundamental attribute of Web3. Web3 aims to offer an alternative to centralized authorities such as large corporations or governments and enable direct P2P interactions \[1,8\]. This structural shift empowers users by eliminating intermediaries, thus decentralizing ownership and control of both digital assets and the infrastructure that supports them (Tapscott, 2023) \[5\].
*   • User sovereignty and empowerment: Empowering users through ownership of their data, digital identities, and assets is a key feature that was highlighted in nearly all sources. Web3 is seen as a framework that allows individuals to regain control over their digital presence, free from surveillance and the control of centralized platforms \[3,6\].
*   • Trustlessness and security: Security and trust in Web3 systems are achieved through cryptographic techniques, decentralized networks, and consensus mechanisms rather than reliance on centralized intermediaries. This feature allows for trustless systems, where transactions and interactions can be executed without the need for parties to know or trust one another \[4\]. The immutability of blockchain records ensures that data and transactions are secure, verifiable, and resistant to tampering \[3,7\].
*   • Transparency and immutability: Web3’s emphasis on transparency is reinforced through its use of public ledgers where all transactions are recorded and available for audit. This ensures a high degree of accountability and censorship resistance, critical in establishing trust in decentralized systems \[7\].
*   • Interoperability: Interoperability refers to Web3’s capacity to create a seamless, integrated user experience across decentralized applications (DApps) and networks. By eliminating the silos of centralized platforms and individual blockchain networks, Web3 fosters a more interconnected digital landscape where users can move freely between different services and platforms \[6\].
*   • Economic democratization and inclusion: Web3 introduces new economic models, particularly through Decentralized Finance (DeFi) and tokenization of assets, that allow for a more inclusive and distributed value creation system (Tapscott, 2023) \[1\]. The elimination of middlemen and gatekeepers reduces barriers to participation and allows individuals from diverse backgrounds to engage directly with global markets and systems of value transfer \[7\].
*   • Community governance through DAOs: Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAOs) are highlighted as a critical innovation in Web3, allowing communities to self-govern and manage digital assets collectively \[3\]. The governance of Web3 is seen as more democratic and participatory, as DAOs provide a structure for community-led decision-making.

#####  2.3.1.1 Decentralization as the cornerstone of Web3

Decentralization is the most universally agreed-upon feature of Web3, fundamentally restructuring how digital interactions occur by shifting from centralized control toward a more distributed, user-centric P2P model, and as such it requires special attention. This feature is at the core of Web3’s value proposition and serves as the foundation upon which many other key attributes of the ecosystem are built. At its essence, decentralization empowers users by removing the need for intermediaries, allowing direct transactions and interactions that promote enhanced data ownership, security, and privacy \[4,5\].

This decentralized structure is not only a technological innovation but also an ideological shift. It reflects a return to the vision of the Internet as a decentralized network, one that was gradually diluted during the rise of centralized platforms and monopolistic corporations in the Web 2.0 era \[6,7\]. Centralized platforms have come to dominate the digital landscape, leading to concerns about data privacy, surveillance, and economic monopolization. Web3, through decentralization, seeks to challenge this concentration of power, offering a more equitable, user-controlled ecosystem where the distribution of power is more balanced.

The importance of decentralization lies in its potential to democratize the digital landscape by redistributing power from centralized authorities to individual users. In this model, users, developers, and other stakeholders interact more equitably, reducing dependency on a few central entities \[8\]. By enabling P2P interactions, Web3 allows users to have greater control over their personal data and digital assets while promoting a more open and transparent ecosystem. The rise of DeFi is an example of this, where financial interactions are no longer mediated by traditional financial institutions. Instead, individuals can participate in inclusive, borderless, and transparent financial systems that operate without centralized control \[1\]. This shift challenges the traditional financial and economic systems, offering new ways of creating and exchanging value globally.

Beyond the economic and financial implications, decentralization has significant socio-cultural and personal effects. It promotes a shift toward more collaborative and participatory digital ecosystems, empowering users to co-create, govern, and control the digital environments and rethink their digital identities, which gains particular importance in the age of AI (Tapscott, 2023).

However, while decentralization is seen as the most fundamental attribute of Web3, many scholars and practitioners acknowledge that this feature is at risk of being undermined. There are growing concerns that Web3 could replicate some of the same centralized power structures of previous digital systems, particularly because of its reliance on centralized physical infrastructure. As noted by Chohan \[1\] and Zheng & Lee \[7\], Web3 systems still depend on centralized entities for critical components, such as Internet service providers (ISPs), data centers, and the energy grid. These centralized control points pose a threat to the decentralization ethos of Web3, as they could allow incumbents from the previous era to maintain or regain control over the new systems.

To address this issue, scholars advocate for a holistic approach to decentralization that encompasses not only digital platforms but also the physical infrastructure supporting them. One such solution is the development of Decentralized Physical Infrastructure Networks (DePIN), which would involve distributed data centers and decentralized energy systems. By decentralizing physical infrastructure at all levels, Web3 can achieve a true P2P transfer of information and value, realizing its full potential as a transformative and democratizing force in the digital age \[7\].

In conclusion, decentralization is not just a technical feature of Web3 but a transformative force reshaping how digital systems operate, interact, and evolve. By empowering users and decentralizing control over data, assets, and infrastructure, Web3 offers the potential for a more inclusive, transparent, and user-driven Internet. However, achieving full decentralization will require addressing the ongoing reliance on centralized physical infrastructure and developing holistic solutions to ensure Web3 lives up to its decentralized ideals.

####  2.3.2 Enabling technologies for decentralization in Web3

As per the reviewed literature, the complexity of achieving true decentralization for P2P communication in Web3 relies on a range of enabling technologies that form the backbone of the Web3 ecosystem. While the literature reveals diverse perspectives on how to categorize and approach these technologies, and some authors \[4,6\] focus on technologies more explicitly than others, a consensus holds that blockchain technologies are at the core of Web3. The term blockchain technologies is used here in the plural to encompass a set of interrelated technologies and solutions that together enable the decentralization necessary for P2P transfer of information. This system, as introduced elsewhere by Nakamoto \[9\], initiated what is widely referred to as the “blockchain revolution” \[10\], which has spawned extensive academic research, practical implementations, and an industry of its own.

While a detailed review of blockchain technologies is beyond the scope of this chapter, it is important to note that not all blockchains are equal.^([²](#fn2))

The reviewed literature identifies the following key components of Web3 blockchain-based technologies.

#####  2.3.2.1 Blockchain

Blockchain is a particular type of database and a subset of Distributed Ledger Technologies (DLT). It records data in an append-only chain of interconnected units, known as blocks. To achieve the desired outcomes of data immutability, security, and P2P interaction, blockchains rely on several key elements:

*   • Cryptographic techniques: These include public and private key mechanisms that secure data and transactions on the blockchain. Cryptography ensures the integrity and authenticity of information in a decentralized system.
*   • Network of interconnected participants (nodes): Blockchain networks consist of multiple nodes that communicate with each other to maintain the integrity of the distributed ledger. Each node acts as both a sender and receiver of information.
*   • Consensus mechanisms: Consensus algorithms, such as Proof of Work and Proof of Stake, ensure that all participants agree on the state of the blockchain. These mechanisms enable secure and decentralized verification of transactions and data integrity across the network.
*   • Tokenized digital assets: Open public blockchains both require and enable the creation of diverse types of digital assets. The blockchain platform's native tokens are referred to as utility tokens and cryptocurrencies. They are integral to the functioning of public blockchains by providing an incentive mechanism for participants to maintain and secure the network. Utility tokens are also needed for the creation of other digital assets—different types of tokens—on blockchains, such as NFTs, tokenized real-world assets, or entire ownable metaverses, which open new opportunities for economic growth in the digital economy.

#####  2.3.2.2 Smart contracts

Smart contracts are self-executing computer programs that automatically enforce the terms of an agreement. Written directly into code, these contracts eliminate the need for intermediaries. Smart contracts power DApps and are the foundation of new governance and economic models such as DAOs and DeFi. These contracts enable automation within decentralized networks, providing an efficient and trustless way to execute agreements securely.

#####  2.3.2.3 Wallets and user interfaces

Wallets serve as user interfaces that allow individuals to securely interact with the blockchain and directly control their digital assets. They act as both the access points for users and the mechanisms by which users maintain ownership and control over their assets in a decentralized system.

#####  2.3.2.4 Decentralized physical infrastructure network (DePIN)

Web3’s decentralization does not only refer to the digital space but also involves DePIN to address the dependence on the centralized infrastructure in the current Web3 \[7\]. While the exact term may not always be featured across the literature, the various elements it contains involve:

*   • Decentralized storage solutions: Examples include the InterPlanetary File System (IPFS), which enables decentralized, P2P storage and file sharing.
*   • Decentralized energy systems: These systems ensure that Web3 remains decentralized at the infrastructural level, reducing reliance on traditional centralized providers of energy.
*   • Internet of Things and Oracles: IoT and Oracles allow for interaction with the physical world and serve as bridges between the blockchain, providing trusted inputs from external sources to smart contracts.
*   • Peer-to-Peer (P2P) networks: Consisting of physical devices, P2P networks allow direct communication between nodes without the need for centralized servers. This helps maintain the decentralized ethos of Web3 while enabling scalable communication systems.

####  2.3.3 Inconsistencies in defining Web3

#####  2.3.3.1 Challenges of defining Web3 technologies

Despite the consensus around several foundational elements of Web3, there remains no unified agreement on the exact set of technologies that constitute Web3. This lack of consensus arises from the rapid pace of technological evolution and differing interpretations within academic and industry literature. For instance, Huang et al. \[4\] advocate for the inclusion of the Semantic Web and Artificial Intelligence (AI) as integral parts of Web3. Conversely, Zheng and Lee \[7\] introduce the concept of “Web3+,” which positions Web3 as a base model and adds additional layers of complexity and technology over time, including advanced AI integration and quantum computing.

Further complicating this issue is the divergent perspective on the role of tokens within Web3. While most scholars consider tokens to be a central feature of Web3, integral to the functioning of blockchain networks and decentralized systems, Zheng and Lee \[7\] argue that tokens should be excluded from the core definition of Web3 and placed within the enhanced framework of “Web3+.” These debates highlight the difficulties of defining Web3’s technological boundaries, especially as new innovations continue to emerge and shape the digital landscape.

#####  2.3.3.2 Inconsistent naming and versioning: The challenge of Web N.0

Another critical challenge in conceptualizing Web3 is the inconsistent use of terms and versioning to describe the evolution of the web. The naming conventions that designate phases of the Internet evolution—such as Web 1.0, Web 2.0, and Web 3.0—are often imprecise and lead to confusion when used interchangeably or jointly with Web1 (…) Web3. For example, Web 1.0 (the 1990s) is commonly understood as the static, read-only phase of the web, where users primarily consumed information without interacting or creating content. Web 2.0 (early 2000s) introduced interactive, read-write capabilities, most famously exemplified by social media platforms and user-generated content. Now, Web 3.0—interchangeably used with Web3—is framed as the phase in which users can read, write, and own content and assets \[5\]. However, this typology tends to conflate the WWW, an information system created by Tim Berners-Lee in 1989 \[11\], with the broader Internet infrastructure \[7\]. This reductionist approach overlooks the Internet's initial purpose and evolution, leading to conceptual gaps.

A more robust, historical understanding, like the one offered by Zheng and Lee \[7\], recognizes the development of the Internet as beginning in the 1960s, which predates the WWW by several decades. The authors also aim to clarify the confusion in naming between Web 3.0 and Web3, with the former originally associated with Tim Berners-Lee and referring to the Semantic Web \[12\]. This concept is built around creating a machine-readable Internet that can understand, analyze, and infer connections within data to improve automation and information sharing (Tapscott, 2023) \[7\]. By contrast, Web3—championed by Gavin Wood, co-founder of Ethereum—relies on blockchain technology and decentralization. In Web3, data is stored in immutable, decentralized structures, secured through cryptographic keys, making it resistant to tampering or deletion. In contrast, Tim Berners-Lee’s response to the need for data privacy and security—as Zheng and Lee \[7\] explain—involves a different set of technologies, Solid Pods. This technological innovation allows users to store and manage data in centralized repositories, allowing data to be amended and updated by the owner or those with authorized access that they manage. This difference highlights the fundamental divergence between different technologies and approaches to security and privacy, even though both terms—Web3 and Web 3.0—are often used incorrectly and interchangeably.

Despite the efforts to clarify the naming in the literature, there remains a need for a more coherent framework that holistically merges both approaches—the evolution of the Internet with the evolution of the WWW.

##  3 Synthesis of findings and author's conclusions

The literature survey on Web3 reveals several critical points that deserve deeper analysis. The primary value of Web3 lies in its potential to decentralize economic and governance power over Internet infrastructure by redistributing it to users. This allows for direct P2P communication and the exchange of digital assets in a censorship-resistant environment. In this framework, users act as sovereign agents, rather than products of sophisticated marketing systems controlled by a few dominant entities. Web3’s decentralized nature promotes inclusivity and openness, granting users the ability to govern their digital activities. Achieving this goal requires a comprehensive technological stack designed to uphold these principles. Thus, there is a need for a grand conceptual framework that positions Web3 as a tool to serve humanity in the digital age, moving beyond technology-dependent versioning. Technology, in this context, should be viewed as a flexible means, an adaptable stack that can evolve to meet Web3’s core goals.

##  4 A new Web3 conceptual framework: Merging Information Theory and Political Economy in a historical context

###  4.1 Information Theory and Web3

At its foundation, Web3 addresses direct communication of information between parties over a network channel. Thus, this chapter proposes a novel way of adapting Information Theory, originally developed by Shannon \[13\] in his seminal work “A Mathematical Theory of Communication,” as an ideal model for conceptualizing Web3’s processes.^([³](#fn3))

In its basic form, Information Theory provides a mathematical explanation of communication as the transfer of a message from an information source through a transmitter to a receiver, over a communication channel, affected by noise \[13\]. The key elements of this theory include:

*   • Information as a quantifiable unit—such as energy, rather than meaning.
*   • Entropy—a measure of uncertainty in the system.
*   • Channels of communication—defining the capacity for information flow.
*   • Redundancy and compression—to cancel out noise and optimize channel capacity.

In his subsequent work, “Communication Theory of Secrecy Systems” (1949), Shannon expanded on how communication can be made private through the mathematical encoding and decoding of messages, laying the groundwork for modern cryptography, which is fundamental to blockchain-based Web3 systems ([Fig. 1](#Ch001_1-15_B9780443347177000076.xhtml#f0010)).

![Fig. 1 Diagram of Shannon's \[13\] communication system.](images/B9780443347177000076/f01-01-9780443347177.jpg)

[Fig. 1](#Ch001_1-15_B9780443347177000076.xhtml#B-f0010) Diagram of Shannon's \[13\] communication system.

The diagram illustrates the communication process with the following components: Information Source, Transmitter, Receiver, Destination, Signal, Received Signal and Noise Source. The process starts with the Information Source, which sends a Message to the Transmitter. The Transmitter converts the Message into a Signal. The Signal is then affected by the Noise Source, resulting in a Received Signal. The Received Signal is sent to the Receiver, which converts it back into a Message. Finally, the Message reaches the Destination.

Here further parallels between Information Theory and Web3’s blockchain technologies—such as Nakamoto's (2008) foundational work—create a coherent framework for conceptualizing Web3. Similar to Information Theory, Web3’s blockchain processes revolve around quantifiable data units stored in blocks of limited capacity (channels) and transmitted from one source to a destination (such as addresses or accounts) across a network. Each node within this network acts as both a sender and receiver. Entropy—or uncertainty—reduces with each additional confirmation of a block (redundancy), minimizing the risk of error or attack (noise) and ensuring the immutability (security) of a record. Privacy (secrecy) is guaranteed by multiple layers of cryptography, while second-layer solutions can further enhance privacy and scalability by increasing the system's capacity.

By applying Information Theory, we can establish a coherent framework for the decentralized web, positioning it within the broader fields of Information and Communication Technologies and the history of the Internet. This approach suggests an evolution away from inconsistent web versioning (e.g., Web 1.0, Web 2.0) and toward a more holistic perspective that incorporates the decentralization of ownership and governance of the communication infrastructure. Since control over information and its infrastructure in the information age equates to both economic and political power, a political economy of communication framework is needed to further understand Web3’s implications.

###  4.2 Political economy and Web3

At its core, the political economy of communication examines how economic and political systems influence communication processes. It focuses on issues such as the ownership of media infrastructure, regulation, and the distribution of power among media stakeholders. Authors like Mosco \[16\] remind us that while new technologies are often celebrated as democratizing tools, they can also entrench existing power imbalances if controlled by corporate or state entities. McChesney \[17,18\] expands on this, demonstrating how the concentration of media and Internet infrastructure in the hands of a few multinational corporations narrows public discourse, threatening democratic processes.

These critiques of the centralized media and communication infrastructure, which preceded Web3, align with the literature reviewed earlier. The political economy framework is particularly useful for identifying key stakeholders in the evolution of the Internet: the state, corporations, and citizens. In an international context, these stakeholders represent competing interests in controlling Internet infrastructure. In the digital economy, the Internet's physical and digital infrastructure can be viewed as a means of production, potentially controlled by any combination of these groups. This framework helps re-examine the Internet's evolution in two distinct phases, as presented by Naughton \[19\], and proposes the next phase, Web3, as a logical extension in the context of political theory. For consistent naming in this conceptual proposal, the first two phases are here named Web1 and Web2, respectively, although these terms are not used in such a way elsewhere.

####  4.2.1 Evolution of the Internet in a historical context: Three phases of control

#####  4.2.1.1 Web1: State-controlled Internet (1950s to mid-1990s)

The Internet began as a state-driven initiative in the United States during the 1950s, originally designed as a communication system resilient to nuclear attacks. The creation of a decentralized mesh network with packet-switching technology by Paul Baran \[20\] and the establishment of the Advanced Research Projects Agency (APRA) marked the early development of Internet infrastructure. APRA connected university computers to the ARPANET for resource sharing, which evolved into a collaborative network. However, governance and ownership remained centralized, and controlled by state actors. The development of TCP/IP protocols in the 1970s and 1980s enabled the interconnection of networks, laying the groundwork for the modern Internet. Civilian control began with the decommissioning of ARPANET, giving rise to commercial ISPs and the Internet's expansion in the 1990s.

#####  4.2.1.2 Web2: Corporate-controlled Internet (mid-1990s to late 2010s)

The commercial Internet emerged in the mid-1990s, characterized by the transition from state-driven to private ownership. This was fueled by two key developments: the Telecommunications Act (1996) in the United States, which privatized network infrastructure, and the invention of the WWW by Tim Berners-Lee \[17\]. The dot-com boom brought speculative investments, creating companies that evolved into modern tech giants. These corporations dominated the Web 2.0 era, raising concerns about centralization, surveillance, and privacy abuses \[21\]. By the mid-2010s, the Internet began to “balkanize,” though blockchain technology, notably absent in Naughton's (2016) analysis, had already planted the seeds for a decentralized Internet with Nakamoto's blockchain project.

#####  4.2.1.3 Web3: User-controlled decentralized Internet (Web3, from the early 2020s)

Though Naughton (2016) does not include this phase, Web3 is proposed as the most plausible next stage. Web3 emerged as a response to the failures of the corporate-controlled phase, in which tech giants exploited user privacy and economic autonomy. Web3 can also be seen as a response to the oppressive control of the Internet by authoritarian states. As the political economy of communication highlights, media and communication infrastructures are subject to control by those who own them \[16\]. The centralization of Internet infrastructure allowed a few corporations to shape information flows, prioritizing their economic interests over public welfare \[17\]. Web3, by decentralizing control over the Internet, offers an opportunity to reverse these trends and create a more democratic, equitable system for the digital economy.

Although the symbolic start of this phase is traced to 2021, its origins can be linked to Nakamoto's (2008) work. The launch of Ethereum in 2014 and Gavin Wood's articulation of Web3 as a decentralized web were key milestones. As decentralized projects mature, bringing higher transparency, security, and institutional adoption, Web3 presents an attractive model for a sustainable political and economic system. However, challenges remain, particularly regarding the centralized control of infrastructure, including data centers, as noted by Mathew \[22\]. The potential of decentralized Internet infrastructure (or DePIN as presented earlier) is crucial to overcoming these challenges, as argued by Zheng and Lee \[7\]. If realized, such technologies may allow the Internet to achieve its democratic potential, not only by decentralizing information but also by redistributing governance and economic power, as some authors proposed \[23,24\].

##  5 A new political economic model for decentralized digital economy and governance: A critical debate

###  5.1 A decentralized ideal

Web3 represents more than just a technological shift; it could provide both the decentralized physical and digital (phygital) infrastructure for true direct democracy and equitable capitalism, where individuals are both users and stakeholders in a system they control. While Web3 enables decentralization at various levels of Internet infrastructure, questions remain as to whether this decentralization allows for broader political and economic governance without intermediaries, or is it a form of a utopian ideal we aspire to? Many early debates surrounding blockchain technologies, which are foundational to Web3, still hold relevance in this space.

Critics argue that decentralized ideals face practical challenges. De Filippi and Loveluck \[25\] distinguish between governance by infrastructure (the protocol) and governance of the infrastructure (the developer community), noting that while protocols may be decentralized, developer communities often remain centralized. Similarly, Walch \[26\] observes that even “trustless” systems still require trust in developers. Furthermore, automated features of smart contracts, which are essential to Web3, do not always align with existing legal frameworks, which remain largely centralized \[27,28\]. Marlinspike \[29\] takes this critique further by highlighting Web3’s reliance on centralized services, arguing that this dependency undermines its potential to deliver a more democratic Internet. Mathew \[22\] also debunks the “myth” of a decentralized Internet, pointing out that even in its early ARPANET stages, the Internet was distributed, not decentralized. He contends that certain necessary centralized governance structures—often unnoticed—are crucial for accountability.

Despite these critiques, Web3 blockchain technology has revolutionized the economy as a foundational infrastructure (Tapscott and Tapscott, 2016) \[30\]. Blockchains enable decentralized governance \[31\], introduce censorship-resistant, unstoppable code \[32\], and establish new standards for global, censorship-resistant currency \[33\]. These technologies provide more than just improved economic efficiency \[34\]; they introduce a new type of institutional technology \[35\] that enables large-scale P2P collaboration, potentially creating a global direct democracy \[7,24\].

###  5.2 Realistic varieties of Web3: A critical reflection

The question remains whether this technological deterministic thinking leads to a natural selection of democracy over other political systems across nations. This question invites the review of one's own biases. The author's upbringing and international life experience have been greatly shaped by various democratic and capitalistic systems. Similarly, much of the literature promoting Web3 as a tool for decentralization of power and democracy stems from authors who share similar experiences. It may well be possible that the fascination with the new possibilities of Web3 technologies extends to the idealization of democratic, political, and economic realities. Agre \[36\], whose work predates Web3 but aligns with its ideals, captures this tension by stating, “The P2P movement understands that architecture is politics, but it should not assume architecture is a substitute for politics.” He argues that while technology can drive institutional change, technologists must better understand institutions. This viewpoint echoes earlier work by Mumford \[37\], who suggested that authoritarian and democratic systems create technologies that serve and replicate their respective political structures. According to this view, decentralized Web3 projects are unlikely to find adoption in authoritarian states. It may be a little productive to try changing some political systems through a form of technological evangelism, as political diversity predates recent technological revolutions. As Sabine and Thorson \[38\] explain in their classic exploration of political theory, governance systems have traditionally been defined by their concentration of power—whether in the hands of an individual, a ruling elite, or the many.

Decentralization, at its core, aligns ideologically with the principles of democracy and diversity. Unlike authoritarian systems that concentrate power, democratic systems—especially those envisioned within the Web3 paradigm—seek to distribute power more equitably among individuals. However, it is important to acknowledge that democracy itself is neither a monolithic concept nor a perfect political system. As Huntington \[39\] and Diamond \[40\] point out, the latter half of the 20th century witnessed several waves of democratization, each adapted to different cultural and temporal contexts. Notably, most democratic systems are indirect, relying on intermediaries and representatives due to the impracticality of direct decision-making in large populations.

Web3, as a technology enabling direct P2P communication and governance at scale, holds the potential to revolutionize contemporary democracy by challenging conventional centers of power. Paradoxically, it is the democratic institutions and leaders advocating for democratic ideals that may face the greatest disruption from Web3 technologies, including AI, which could facilitate more efficient and participatory forms of direct democracy.

If political power can be seen as existing on a spectrum between centralized and decentralized forms of governance. The same holds true for economic systems of ownership. Hall and Soskice's \[41\] Varieties of Capitalism offers a useful political-economic framework for recognizing differences between more collectively coordinated market economies (CME), such as Germany or China, and liberal market economies, such as the United States. The differing characteristics of each political-economic system align with the governance structures of various blockchain technologies \[42\]. Blockchains that show higher levels of centralized control and governance are often referred to as DLTs and in this sense may ideologically align with CMEs. Blockchains with a higher level of decentralization, on the other hand, fit more logically into the less regulated LMS. A perfectly decentralized Web3 system can be compared to an economic system that does not involve any centralized intervention, like Ronald Coase's \[43\] distinction between a firm and an economic system. Although various attempts have been made throughout history, a perfectly free market system has not materialized yet. Hence, acknowledging the diversity in political-economic systems allows for a more nuanced understanding of the different approaches to implementing Web3 technologies across borders. Recognizing these distinctions and one's own biased thinking can prevent conceptual misunderstandings.

##  6 Web3 Tech Stack

By conceptualizing Web3 here, it is essential to recognize that the goal is not merely to pursue the latest technological trend but to view Web3 as a new platform designed to build a more equitable and inclusive decentralized digital economy in the 21st century. Technology serves only as a tool to achieve this human-centric goal, and while blockchain technologies are foundational, they will likely converge with other emerging technologies to form what can be best described here as the Web3 Tech Stack.

Currently, technologies that influence this stack the most, besides blockchain, include AI, IoT, and quantum computing. Numerous studies demonstrate that the convergence of blockchain with AI and IoT can streamline operations, improve efficiency, enhance security, and add economic value to businesses \[44,45\]. Furthermore, decentralized AI enhances data privacy through federated learning models, which allow systems to securely store local data while maintaining privacy \[46\]. Following this line of development, open, public, blockchain-based Web3 solutions may soon represent humanity's best option for securely and ethically controlling AI.

A mutually beneficial relationship also exists between blockchains and quantum computing. While quantum computers could theoretically threaten cryptography used in blockchain systems, they also provide the potential for quantum-resistant blockchains. These enhanced blockchains could bolster system security even further by eliminating central points of failure \[47–49\]. However, many of these solutions remain theoretical, and the true impact of quantum computing on Web3 systems will only become apparent once quantum computers enter commercial use.

To better clarify the distinction between Web3 technologies and centralized Internet infrastructure, the following typology offers an attempt to delineate the differences. Jackson's \[50\] comprehensive overview of web technologies is adapted here to provide a point of reference. Simply put, Jackson's \[50\] system consists of three main elements: web browsers used to access the web, servers to store and supply information, and the computer network supporting browser-server communication. These elements are further supported by protocols and software ([Table 1](#Ch001_1-15_B9780443347177000076.xhtml#t0010)).

[Table 1](#Ch001_1-15_B9780443347177000076.xhtml#B-t0010)

Comparative presentation of centralized vs. decentralized Internet infrastructure.

 
| Component || Traditional centralized architecture—examples || Web3 decentralized architecture—examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Physical networks || Cables, fiber optics, routers, switches || Same physical infrastructure and DePIN (Decentralized Physical Infrastructure Networks); utilized by blockchains and nodes |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  || Managed by centralized ISPs || Managed by decentralized nodes for peer-to-peer communication |
| Servers and data centers || Centralized servers and data centers managed by ISPs, cloud providers (e.g., AWS, Google Cloud) || Distributed nodes storing data across a decentralized network; decentralized data storage (IPFS, Filecoin) |
| Protocols || TCP/IP, DNS, HTTP/HTTPS, FTP || Blockchain protocols (e.g., Ethereum, Bitcoin), decentralized name services (ENS, Handshake) |
| Client-side technologies || Web browsers (Chrome, Firefox, Safari) || Web3-enabled browsers or extensions (Brave, MetaMask), Metaverse |
| Applications || Centralized apps reliant on back-end servers || Decentralized apps (dApps) and direct blockchain interactions via Web3 wallets (MetaMask, WalletConnect) |
| Server-side technologies || Server-side scripting languages (PHP, Python, Ruby, etc.) || Smart contracts (e.g., Solidity for Ethereum) that automate processes on the blockchain |
| Databases || Centralized databases (MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle DB) || Blockchains as decentralized databases, enabling immutable, trustless data storage and transfer |
| Web frameworks and APIs || Traditional frameworks (Django, Laravel, Rails) || Web3 frameworks (Truffle Suite, Web3.js, Ethers.js) that integrate blockchain functionalities into dApps |
|  || APIs for centralized services || Decentralized APIs and oracles for interacting with blockchain and decentralized services |
| Security layers || SSL/TLS encryption, firewalls, centralized authentication (OAuth, Single Sign-On) || Cryptographic signatures, decentralized identity systems (self-sovereign identity), zero-knowledge proofs |
| AI integration || Centralized AI services (e.g., cloud-based platforms like Google AI, AWS AI) || Decentralized AI models on blockchain (e.g., SingularityNET), using blockchain for data integrity, privacy, and decentralized processing |
| IoT integration || Centralized IoT platforms managed by cloud providers (Azure IoT, AWS IoT) || Decentralized IoT networks using blockchain for secure device communication (IOTA, IoTeX) |
| Quantum computing integration || Quantum computing assisting traditional supercomputers with complex problems || Quantum-resistant cryptographic algorithms to safeguard blockchain against quantum threats, enhancing security and transaction speed |

The table above illustrates the key differences between traditional centralized architecture and Web3’s decentralized architecture across various technological components. Web3 redefines ownership, trust, and interaction on the web by empowering users to control their data and digital identities directly, without reliance on centralized intermediaries. This shift from centralized entities (e.g., ISPs, cloud providers) to decentralized systems managed by users and networks of peers has profound implications not only for technological infrastructure but also for the political economy, as it decentralizes governance, data storage, and decision-making. These changes align with the broader aims of digital sovereignty and inclusion discussed above.

##  7 Implications

Building on these foundations, Web3 has far-reaching societal, economic, cultural, and personal implications, particularly concerning privacy, identity, and control in the digital age (Tapscott, 2023). Although decentralization within Web3 is not yet fully realized, ongoing efforts like DePIN are crucial for further decentralizing infrastructure. They will also enhance trustless and transparent systems such as DAOs and DeFi \[7\]. These developments pave the way for inclusive and equitable economies, offering new opportunities for sustainable growth. Furthermore, the immersive Web3 Metaverse can unlock limitless possibilities for economic creativity and digital ownership, often more sustainable than the physical world, especially when built on renewable and regenerative infrastructures \[51,52\].

Web3 offers a unique convergence of direct democracy and capitalism by enabling tokenized ownership of digital assets and infrastructure. This creates a more inclusive economy, where the means of production are owned and controlled by the stakeholders, reducing traditional hierarchies of power. Furthermore, Web3 has the potential to redefine power dynamics between the state, capital, and labor. Individuals could have direct control over the digital economy, while automation facilitates the secure scaling of democratic governance. In the age of AI, Web3 represents one of the best mechanisms to prevent the monopolization of AI by corporations or governments. By democratically owning and governing AI, society can ensure that powerful technologies like AGI (Artificial General Intelligence) remain under human control.

Despite its promise, Web3 faces challenges such as misinformation, regulatory hurdles, and exploitation. Misinformation, as noted by Tapscott and Tapscott (2016), is a strategy used by incumbents to usurp the technology. This can manifest in various ways, such as exaggerating the negative aspects of blockchain technologies while ignoring larger issues with traditional systems. Moreover, regulation, while needed for consumer protection, risks stifling innovation by reinforcing existing power structures, potentially leading to the monopolization of new technologies. Critics like Marlinspike \[29\] and Chohan \[1\] caution that if Web3 merely replicates centralized power structures, its revolutionary potential could be lost. Furthermore, the significance of Web3 as a transformational political-economic system for P2P interaction in the digital age may be overlooked in the narratives of Web N.0 versioning, such as Web 4.0, which often focuses on chasing the next big tech trend for marketing reasons.

Moving forward, the key to harnessing Web3’s potential lies in responsible adoption and the development of regulatory frameworks that protect users while encouraging innovation. This can be achieved through:

*   • Education and awareness: Ensuring that users understand the technology and its associated risks.
*   • Regulation: Developing policies that protect against fraud while fostering innovation.
*   • Community engagement: Encouraging the development of community-led initiatives that reflect the true spirit of decentralization and empowerment.
*   • Web3 standards: Developing a coherent international standard for Web3 to enable seamless cross-border integration and communication.

##  8 Conclusion

This chapter proposed a comprehensive and interdisciplinary framework for conceptualizing Web3, moving beyond the current, inconsistent versioning of Web N.0. Through a review of the literature, the chapter identified the key features and technologies of Web3, along with potential inconsistencies. Building on this analysis, it was proposed to conceptualize Web3 through the lens of Information Theory and Political Economy as a phygital, decentralized Internet infrastructure enabling P2P communication, governance, and the creation and ownership of digital assets and the infrastructure. The historical evolution of the Internet from the perspective of infrastructure ownership revealed three phases of control by key stakeholders: the state, corporations, and the people—the core users of Web3. From a political-economic perspective, the Web3 infrastructure is proposed here as a new means of production in the digital age where Web3, more broadly defined, is equivalent to a new political and economic system, enabling direct P2P value creation and exchange within the 21st-century digital economy. Importantly, in the age of advancing AI developments, Web3 could represent humanity's best hope for ensuring control and maintaining a more equitable digital future.

# Chapter 2 Blockchain interoperability for decentralized finance

1.  Li Yuxian
2.  Jinan University, Guangzhou, China

## Abstract

With the rapid development of decentralized finance (DeFi), blockchain interoperability has become a crucial factor driving innovation in this field. This chapter explores the importance, challenges, and solutions associated with this topic. First, we examine the definition and role of interoperability in DeFi, emphasizing its necessity for achieving seamless asset movement and cross-platform connectivity. Second, we analyze the interoperability challenges faced by the current DeFi landscape, including the lack of standardization among different blockchain networks, the technical complexity of cross-chain communication, and the consistency issues of smart contracts. Next, we delve into emerging solutions such as relay chains, cross-chain protocols, and standardization efforts to facilitate broader connectivity within the DeFi ecosystem. Finally, we highlight the significance of blockchain interoperability in realizing more open, accessible, and innovative financial services. We underscore the collaborative efforts needed from both the industry and academia to drive the standardization of interoperability. This chapter provides a comprehensive understanding of the theme “Blockchain interoperability for decentralized finance,” highlighting its critical role in advancing the development of the DeFi ecosystem.

DeFi

Interoperability

Blockchain

##  1 Introduction

###  1.1 Brief explanation of blockchain interoperability

The development of blockchain technology (cf. [Fig. 1](#Ch002_17-33_B9780443347177000106.xhtml#f0010)) can be divided into three main stages, each representing significant advancements in technology and application areas. Specifically, Blockchain 3.0 focuses on a broader range of applications, including improved scalability and cross-chain interoperability. Blockchain interoperability refers to the ability of different blockchains to seamlessly communicate and share data \[1–3\]. After the appearance of Bitcoin in 2008, various blockchain platforms have surfaced, each tailored with distinctive characteristics, such as different privacy measures, and different consensus mechanisms like proof of stake \[4\] or proof of work \[5\]. Yet, the autonomous operation of these blockchains often results in a fragmented ecosystem, hindering interoperability. Interoperability is crucial for overcoming these siloes by establishing protocols and standards that pave the way for compatibility and interplay among different blockchain architectures.

![Fig. 1 The blockchain technology development.](images/B9780443347177000106/f02-01-9780443347177.jpg)

[Fig. 1](#Ch002_17-33_B9780443347177000106.xhtml#B-f0010) The blockchain technology development.

The flowchart depicts the evolution of blockchain technology through three stages. The first stage is Blockchain 1.0, which includes bitcoin and zerocash. The second stage is Blockchain 2.0, which features Ethereum Smart Contract. The third stage is Blockchain 3.0, which focuses on Blockchain Interoperability.

To release the communication gap between blockchains, some solutions so-called *bridges or hubs* have been developed \[6, 7\]. These bridges serve as intermediaries and enable users to transfer assets and information across blockchain platforms. An example includes the interoperability that cross-chain DeFi platforms like Cosmos \[8\] and Polkadot \[9\] are forging paths for interoperable blockchain networks, where a smart contract on Ethereum can trigger actions on other chains, expanding the capabilities of decentralized applications (DApps). For example, a DApp for supply chain management could leverage the transparency of Ethereum for contract execution while utilizing the privacy features of another blockchain, like Monero, for sensitive data handling. Specifically, the construction of interoperability infrastructure not only promotes efficiency within the blockchain ecosystem but also fosters an environment that is more beneficial from innovation. By allowing for the fluid movement of assets and data, such infrastructure supports the emergence of an accessible and synergistic digital economy.

Standardization plays an important role in the progression of blockchain technologies \[10\]. Common protocols and interfaces are akin to a universal language, facilitating clear and effective communication between various blockchains. Initiatives like the Interledger Protocol \[11\] seek to provide a standard of application programming interfaces (APIs) for interoperability, while the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C) is working on standards for enabling secure and verifiable cross-chain transactions. Such efforts are keys in shaping a unified blockchain ecosystem, which is critical for stimulating innovation and collaborative development.

In essence, blockchain interoperability is not simply a technical feature but also a foundational element that will determine the capacity of the blockchain landscape to thrive. It dismisses the barriers between blockchain networks, fostering a climate of cooperation, standardization, and interconnectedness. As the blockchain domain matures, achieving interoperability will be vital to unlocking the full potential of decentralized technologies, thereby contributing to a digital infrastructure on a worldwide scale.

###  1.2 Brief explanation of decentralized finance

Decentralized finance (DeFi) \[12, 13\] represents a novel financial paradigm, fundamentally transforming the traditional finance mechanisms. It utilizes blockchain and smart contract technologies to establish a financial ecosystem independent of centralized institutions. The primary goal of DeFi is to harness the decentralization and transparency of blockchain, making financial services more accessible and efficient, and enhancing user control and privacy.

Smart contracts, the core technology in DeFi, are self-executing and immutable contracts with the terms of the agreement directly written into code \[4\]. Unlike traditional financial services, DeFi operates directly through contract code without relying on centralized financial institutions. Initially, DeFi development was largely focused on Ethereum, primarily due to its support for complex smart contracts. As the technology evolved and gained market recognition, DeFi started attracting more attention, especially in 2020, named the “Year of DeFi,” when the total value locked (TVL)^([⁴](#fn4))
