# Chapter 4 Navigating cryptocurrencies’ next frontier: The revolution toward decentralizing physical infrastructure

1.  Jincheng Zheng
2.  Swee-Won Lo
3.  Chongwu Xia
4.  David Kuo Chuen Lee
5.  School of Business, Singapore University of Social Sciences, Singapore, Singapore

## Abstract

Since 2023, Decentralized Physical Infrastructure Networks (DePINs) have emerged, utilizing blockchain to transform centralized infrastructure systems. DePIN integrates cryptocurrencies and the Internet of Things (IoT) to develop traditional industries and the new digital economy. This article outlines DePIN's concept, mechanisms, applications, and future trends, as well as current noteworthy challenges. The LASIC principle is used to measure the feasibility of DePIN, guiding industrial practitioners in the correct directions to focus on. This article also compares various public blockchains that are developing DePIN and proposes criteria for cultivating a prosperous DePIN ecosystem. The purpose of this chapter is to offer comprehensive guidance to those interested in using blockchain for cost-effective services and to update scholars on cryptocurrency advancements.

## Keywords

DePIN

Blockchain

Cryptocurrency

Decentralization

Bitcoin

LASIC

Internet of things

##  1 The concept of decentralized physical infrastructure network (DePIN)

Over the past few years, the rise of blockchain technology and cryptocurrencies has shifted the way that people interact with each other from the offline to the online world. The decentralized nature of blockchain has transformed every aspect of our digital lives, from GameFi and decentralized social networking to other scenarios. However, it is critical to note that this revolution is not limited to the virtual realm. Some practitioners and policymakers have begun to focus on DePIN, with the intention of using cryptocurrencies to promote the growth of the real sector.

DePIN emerges as an innovative paradigm that utilizes blockchain technology and token economics to facilitate the creation and management of distributed physical infrastructure systems. DePINs utilize smart contracts and blockchain technology to enable autonomous real-time interactions within the physical infrastructure of the Internet of Things (IoT), accelerating the system's responsiveness to human requirements and improving its adaptability. The idea was first introduced by IoTeX \[1\] as MachineFi. Messari (2022) first coined the term “DePIN” in its report after conducting a Twitter poll ([https://twitter.com/MessariCrypto/status/1588938954807869440?ref=iotex.io](https://twitter.com/MessariCrypto/status/1588938954807869440?ref=iotex.io)). According to Connor \[2\], the DePIN sector's total addressable market is approximately US$2.2 trillion and could reach US$3.5 trillion by 2024. This number is three times the market capitalization of all cryptocurrencies today. DePIN paves the way for a fresh approach to managing services and infrastructure.

DePIN aims to address the pain points of centralized physical infrastructure deployment and management that large corporations dominate due to high capital requirements and logistical challenges. These centralized entities have a near-monopoly on pricing and services offered to end users. DePIN aims to democratize the provision of essential services by granting equitable access and participation opportunities to individuals and smaller entities in the deployment and governance of infrastructure networks. In other words, it is predicated on the principles of decentralization and collective ownership. Moreover, the services or products provided by DePIN are more transparent and trustworthy as blockchain stores verifiable data. In addition, DePIN provides the potential to fully utilize idle resources like computing power and storage space in an economically efficient way. [Table 1](#Ch004_51-59_B9780443347177000180.xhtml#t0010) compares the differences between DePIN and centralized infrastructure.

[Table 1](#Ch004_51-59_B9780443347177000180.xhtml#B-t0010)

A side-by-side comparison of DePIN versus traditional centralized infrastructure.

 
| DePIN || Centralized infrastructure |
| --- | --- |
| Fair access for providers to participate in price competition || Dominance in pricing and services |
| --- | --- |
| Provide transparent and trustworthy data || Not disclosing data externally or utilizing data internally for their own benefit |
| Minimal entry barriers through utilizing idle resources mainly || Substantial initial capital investments |
| Innovative experimentation with open source || Patent protection and slow progress of innovation |
| Use token incentives to bootstrap cheaply and quickly || Inefficient operations and high-cost marketing |
| Decentralized nodes provide a more resilient network || Single point of failure risk |

##  2 The mechanism of DePIN

Traditional giants usually use large amounts of subsidies to attract users when they want to promote products or services that would strain the health of their financial reserves. As a result, some companies may fail after spending their budget, while others may charge high fees after dominating the market.

DePIN emerges by utilizing cryptocurrencies to solve the pain points of bootstrapping new projects. DePIN achieves this by coordinating various essential components:

1.  1. Products or services. In 2023, there are over 650 DePIN projects across six subsectors: computing (250), AI (200), wireless (100), sensors (50), energy (50), and services (25) \[3\].
2.  2. Suppliers: Companies or individuals provide more cost-efficient services or underutilized resources with the expectation of getting token rewards.
3.  3. Consumers: Companies or individuals buy or use products and services.
4.  4. Token economics: DePIN projects use token rewards to attract suppliers to contribute to the system and subsidize consumers.
5.  5. Physical infrastructures: The devices used by suppliers to provide services.

DePIN is collectively deployed and maintained by a global network of individual and corporate contributors. The decentralized and autonomous system for maintaining and improving physical infrastructure is enabled using token incentives. Contributors earn tokens by contributing labor, materials, or other resources toward the infrastructure's provision, maintenance, and improvement. The tokens can, in turn, be used to access the infrastructure or be traded on exchanges. The key is tokenization to coordinate and incentivize the bootstrapping phase and build the network. As more and more users use the product or service, the protocol's revenue increases. Part of the revenue can be used for market capitalization management and further marketing. DePIN projects typically require payment for services via network tokens. As adoption increases, the demand to purchase tokens increases, driving up the price of tokens and further incentivizing providers to contribute to the network. Tokens had a flywheel effect on the DePIN project during the bull market.

DePIN can be considered an innovative way to raise funding in a permissionless and borderless manner using cryptocurrencies. The blockchain serves as the settlement layer for DePIN. By harnessing the power of blockchain technology, smart contracts, and tokens, these networks enable trustless transactions and incentivize individuals to contribute to the infrastructure industry in a permissionless, trustless, and programmatic way.

##  3 DePIN feasibility analysis with LASIC principles

The LASIC principles outline five key success factors of fintech companies to create a sustainable business for financial inclusion, which include low profit margin, asset light, scalability, innovative, and ease of compliance \[4\]. [Table 2](#Ch004_51-59_B9780443347177000180.xhtml#t0015) explains each factor separately.

[Table 2](#Ch004_51-59_B9780443347177000180.xhtml#B-t0015)

The factors of LASIC principles.

 
| Low profit margin || Low initial margin to build adoption and create exponential multiple revenue streams such as advertising, complementary products, or consumer data analytics |
| --- | --- |
| Asset light || Without high fixed costs to support the low-margin principle |
| Scalability || Be scalable to obtain the benefits of network effects |
| Innovative || Be innovative in projects and operations |
| Ease of compliance || Low compliance requirements can boost innovation and reduce capital investments |

DePIN is a category of fintech companies; therefore, we will use the LASIC principles to study its feasibility.

Compared to a centralized infrastructure, the price of the services or products offered by DePIN is much lower. This is because they do not need to invest large sums of money to start a project. Most DePIN projects seek to match the demand and supply of existing infrastructure so that idle resources can be fully utilized. As a result, the assets of DePIN projects are low, giving them a cost advantage over centralized facilities. In order to attract users, the profit margin of DePIN is very low, even offering token incentives or subsidies. Consumers are encouraged to try new alternatives because of the better economic benefits. Take Akash, for example. It is a decentralized cloud computing platform that allows users to effectively trade idle computing power. The cost of using Akash is only about one-third the cost of Amazon AWS, Google Cloud Platform, and Microsoft Azure ([https://akash.network/about/pricing/custom/](https://akash.network/about/pricing/custom/)).

The network of DePIN can be scalable as the decentralized structure lowers the entry barrier, and the products they offer are welcomed by consumers. Besides that, the flywheel effect of tokens in [Section 2](#Ch004_51-59_B9780443347177000180.xhtml#s0015) plays an important role in scaling DePIN projects.

DePIN projects bring innovations to many important existing industries, which are not workable by centralized infrastructures. We will cover some famous use cases in [Section 4](#Ch004_51-59_B9780443347177000180.xhtml#s0025).

Decentralized finance is considered the first successful real-world application of blockchain technology and cryptocurrencies. The next important direction that builders are focusing on is the DePIN project, which is being actively developed in crypto-friendly areas. These areas have allowed the DePIN project to undergo trials to determine if it can help with economic development and bring real benefits to individuals and society in daily life. However, DePIN projects may face challenges in meeting compliance requirements in areas where cryptocurrencies are banned. In such cases, they may have to suspend or discontinue business development activities.

DePIN projects meet most of the factors of the LASIC principle, except for easing compliance in some areas. The use of blockchains and cryptocurrencies to develop virtual and real-world economies is a trend that cannot be ignored or stopped. Blockchain technology will improve the lives of ordinary people through DePIN, following its success in bringing value storage through Bitcoin and decentralized applications through Ethereum. DePIN expands the application of blockchain technology outside financial inclusion to many other industries seeking more resilient, transparent, and cost-effective solutions. Therefore, it is foreseeable that DePIN will be accepted by more countries and regions, and related regulations will be launched. Regulations do not mean to hinder the development of the industry. Appropriate regulations can guide builders with long-term ambitions to take the right actions and deter speculators. Therefore, DePIN has the potential to be as successful as other fintech companies based on the assessment of LASIC principles.

##  4 Public blockchains developing DePIN

DePIN is a product of the combination of blockchain and the Internet of Things. Therefore, a suitable underlying blockchain is crucial for the operation of DePIN projects.

###  4.1 Solana

Solana is a general-purpose layer 1 blockchain that has developed a thriving DePIN ecosystem, with well-known projects including Helium, Render, [io.net](http://io.net), and Hivemapper. The fast development of the DePIN projects on Solana is due to its low transaction costs, fast transaction speed, and scalability, providing a user-friendly experience for its users. As the most active ecosystem outside of the Ethereum ecosystem, the trading volume of DeFi and NFT on Solana has surpassed Ethereum multiple times. The number of active users and the volume of total value locked, in turn, contribute to the development of the project. Solana, as a high-performance layer 1 blockchain, does not need layer 2 rollups to meet performance requirements. Therefore, there is no issue of liquidity fragmentation in the Solana network. The programmability of Solana token extensions provides its developers with more flexibility, allowing them to design specific features for tokens as needed. This top-down approach contrasts sharply with the other blockchains. Solana's uniqueness lies in its pioneering launch of the Web3 phone, reflecting its emphasis on mobile networks. This helps to cultivate consumer usage habits and promote the mass adoption of cryptocurrencies in daily life through the use of mobile phones. Helium provides Solana mobile users with a free 1-month service, which not only motivates users to use the Solana network but also cultivates new users for itself. Solana mobile phones have opened up new channels for acquiring Web3 users. The Solana Foundation and venture capital firms such as Multicoin firmly support DePIN by opening hackathons and providing active grants to attract more outstanding developers to build projects on Solana.

###  4.2 IoTeX

IoTeX is a DePIN-specific purpose layer 1, aimed at building a decentralized IoT data platform that provides privacy protection, security, and scalability for IoT devices. Its technological innovation includes using a unique blockchain-in-blockchain architecture, allowing multiple independent subchains to run on the main chain, each of which can be optimized for different IoT application scenarios. In addition, through the W3bstream protocol, IoTeX has implemented ZK-based on-chain and off-chain interaction, allowing IoT devices or dApps to process and compute data off-chain and submit the results for on-chain verification, achieving verifiable computation and data privacy protection. Besides, the introduction of TEE technology ensures the secure execution of smart contracts.

###  4.3 GM network

GM Network is the first modular DePIN-specific purpose layer 2 on Ethereum. It attempts to build a data network platform by linking DePIN hardware and further combining it with artificial intelligence (AI) to generate personalized AI agents. The entire GM Network ecosystem includes five parts: GM Chain, GM ID, GM Launchpad, GM OS, and GM AI. Among them, GM Chain uses OP Stack and Altlayer to build a modular layer 2 solution for Ethereum, achieving high performance, scalability, and low cost while utilizing EigenLayer to provide decentralized secure computing and data privacy protection.

###  4.4 MXC

The original intention of MXC was to use blockchain technology to solve the problem of low, insecure data exchange efficiency of the Internet of Things and improve transparency. To address the challenge of maintaining efficient network operation as more devices connect to the network, MXC has built a DePIN-focused layer 3 that is compatible with ZkEVM under the Arbitrum. This ensures the security and stability of data transmission among IoT nodes. MXC is also the first layer 3 blockchain ecosystem built on Arbitrum, using project tokens as gas fees. The layer 3 ecosystem is designed to operate independently of other applications, ensuring predictable performance and cost. Meanwhile, roll-up transactions do not need to be sent directly to layer 1, resulting in lower costs.

Overall, to consider whether a blockchain is suitable for developing DePIN, it is necessary to check whether it meets the following criteria:

1.  1. **Low cost**. A low-cost blockchain is more inclusive, which benefits users by reducing the cost burden of user interaction applications. This is also the reason why the DePIN project cannot take place on the Ethereum main network.
2.  2. **High performance**. For a blockchain to gain acceptance among users, it is crucial that it can efficiently process transaction requests and provide a user-friendly experience.
3.  3. **The number of active users**. The number of active users is a prerequisite for the development of the DePIN project. If there are not many users on a blockchain, then the base of users who use DePIN products is relatively small. It is even more difficult to attract new users outside of the blockchain.
4.  4. **Strategic positioning**. The strategic positioning of a blockchain is crucial for the DePIN project since it relies on blockchain. It is more conducive to obtaining resource support during the development process to choose a blockchain that supports DePIN strongly.
5.  5. **Prosperity**. The basic infrastructure of blockchain, such as DeFi and cross-chain bridges, the culture of ecological projects, and whether investors have gained profits are all factors that DePIN projects should focus on.

##  5 DePIN use cases

The categories of DePIN can be separated into virtual and physical resources, comprising various subindustries such as wireless networks, sensors, computing resources, bandwidth, artificial intelligence, storage, and other daily use scenarios. We cover some real-world cases in this section.

###  5.1 Decentralized storage

Centralized storage typically relies on one or a handful of key servers that hold all the data in one place. If these servers fail or are attacked, the availability of the entire system is compromised. DePIN offers a more secure, resilient, and cost-effective solution in the data storage domain by distributing data across multiple nodes (i.e., contributors), thereby eliminating the risk associated with a single point of failure in centralized storage systems.

In addition to security, decentralized storage is more affordable. According to Lim \[5\], 1 TB of storage per month costs US$2.11 on average in decentralized storage protocols, while large centralized storage companies charge up to US$9.88. On average, decentralized storage is 78.6% cheaper than centralized storage. The distinguished difference is because decentralized storage uses idle resources, which do not require much upfront investment.

An example of DePIN for decentralized storage is Filecoin. Filecoin offers cloud storage services similar to those offered by Amazon Web Services and Google Cloud. Filecoin is built on top of the InterPlanetary File System (IPFS), which introduces content-addressable storage (Content-addressable storage is a way of storing information so that it can be retrieved according to its content, rather than its location or name.) that is location-agnostic and allows greater resiliency, easier data portability, and lower latency when computation is involved.

Using the blockchain crypto-economic design principle, Filecoin connects those needing space to store data with contributors with spare space on their hard drives. Contributors who provide storage space are paid with the FIL token. The rapid growth of storage capacity on Filecoin (14 EiB in 2 years) provides affirmation that crypto-economic incentives have been effective at coordinating globally distributed parties to bootstrap a network. Messari's DePIN Sector Map ([https://messari.io/report/the-depin-sector-map?referrer=all-research&ref=iotex.io](https://messari.io/report/the-depin-sector-map?referrer=all-research&ref=iotex.io).) states that Filecoin is currently the largest storage network.

Besides Filecoin, there are several strong competitors providing decentralized storage, solutions including Arweave, BNB Greenfield, EthStorage, and Storj.

###  5.2 Decentralized wireless network

In the realm of internet connectivity, DePIN's decentralized network of hotspots could democratize internet access, providing coverage in underserved areas that traditional telecom companies often overlook due to the high costs and logistical hurdles of infrastructure deployment.

Building a wireless network requires a large capital investment and is therefore usually monopolized by a few large, well-funded companies. Decentralized Wireless Network: In the early stages of development, revenue paid by subscribers may not be sufficient to sustain operations. The protocol uses token rewards to encourage and support providers in purchasing and deploying equipment and sustaining operations. As more providers and consumers join, the economies of scale will lead to lower costs and increased revenue streams for providers, wider coverage of network services, and ultimately a sustainable economic system.

The most famous early example of a DePIN is Helium, which launched a decentralized wireless network (DeWi) in 2019 supported by individuals running interconnected hardware devices worldwide. Helium was founded in 2013 to make it easier to build decentralized wireless networks. The Helium Network Token (HNT) is the protocol token of the Helium network. It can be redeemed by hotspot hosts and operators when they deploy and maintain network coverage. Enterprises and developers should pay HNT to connect devices and build applications on the Helium network.

The telecommunications industry operates with two models: Mobile Virtual Network Operators (MVNOs) and Mobile Network Operators (MNOs). MVNOs have customer relationships but without essential physical infrastructure such as mobile towers. They pay fees to MNOs so that customers can utilize MNOs's infrastructure. Helium's subsidiary project, Helium Mobile, has emerged as a decentralized 5G operator, introducing a new category called MHNO (Mobile Hybrid Network Operator). The $Mobile token incentivizes network participants to deploy and operate 5G mobile network hardware, enabling customers to utilize cellular and Wi-Fi hotspots within the Helium network.

Helium Mobile subscribers can roam to a Helium Mobile hotspot when they are within range. Helium Mobile compensates contributors who set up and maintain hotspots with $HNT, a portion of which is subsequently burned. In areas not covered by the Helium network, Helium Mobile pays higher T-Mobile fees to facilitate users roaming onto T-Mobile's mobile towers, ensuring nationwide high-quality coverage. Helium Mobile users can join the decentralized telecommunications network by contributing hotspots to improve signals in poorly covered areas. Users can purchase Helium Mobile hotspot devices to become providers. Providers can utilize the network and earn rewards when others use it.

The primary cost of constructing 5G networks is building base stations. Helium Mobile utilizes token-based economic incentives to encourage individuals to purchase hotspot facilities and deploy them indoors and outdoors. This mobilizes the collective power of the masses, replacing large-scale base stations with numerous decentralized small hotspots. This approach results in lower construction costs, broader network coverage, and more affordable telecommunications plans. The average monthly expenditure on wireless plans for US users in 2023 was US$157 \[6\]. However, Helium Mobile offers plans with unlimited calls, data, and texts nationwide for only US$20 per month. In Miami, they even offer a remarkable US$5 monthly plan.

The deployment of DePIN for internet access is vital for many reasons. In areas with low population density, the traditional methods of establishing connectivity are expensive and challenging due to the costs associated with infrastructure development, such as erecting radio towers in geographically challenging locations. These costs are often passed on to the end users, increasing the economic burden. Moreover, conventional connectivity methods typically rely on centralized systems, which are susceptible to a single point of failure, potentially disrupting service for numerous users. In contrast, DePIN offers a more resilient and cost-effective solution, decentralizing internet access and reducing the risk of widespread outages.

###  5.3 Renewable energy

As we move toward a sustainable and green future, having secure and reliable carbon credits recorded on an immutable blockchain becomes ever so important. The Arkreen Network is an example of such a solution. Arkreen builds a network to economically collect trustless distributed renewable energy generation data and convert the data into a Renewable Energy Certificate (REC) for sale to anyone who wants to claim carbon neutrality. Arkreen Network leverages Internet of Things (IoT) and blockchain connectivity for easy access and focuses on solar photovoltaics (PV) for mass adoption. It offers embedded and integrated IoT connection options for scalability. With these, a distributed renewable energy resources infrastructure can be built up. Similar to all DePIN solutions, a token-incentivized global coordination method is deeply applied to bootstrap Arkreen in a bottom-up way.

Starpower is a platform that plays a key role in the Virtual Power Plant (VPP) workflow, acting as a hub for information transfer between global Distributed Energy Resources (DERs) and local VPP service providers. By collecting and meticulously analyzing DER data from across the globe, Starpower improves the efficiencies of VPP service providers. The analysis guides service providers to trade and manage power on their local grids, optimizing resource allocation, reducing energy costs, and helping to drive wider renewable energy adoption. Starpower's role helps the electricity market operate at a more granular level, delivering a win-win situation in terms of both economic and environmental benefits. Using decentralized blockchain technology, Starpower greatly enhances the security, stability, and transparency of the electricity network, thus providing a safer and more reliable service to users.

###  5.4 Decentralized computing network

The emergence of blockchain and AI continues to increase the demand for computing resources. In addition, the recent boom in AI development has dramatically increased the demand for chips, which are often in short supply.

Distributed computing networks offer an alternative to solutions dominated by centralized cloud providers and hardware manufacturers. Distributed computing networks use token incentives to attract computing power providers to offer idle computing resources to help users perform complex computing tasks, such as running artificial intelligence algorithms and analyzing large data sets. By eliminating the need for providers to invest extra money to provide computing power to the network, it lowers the barrier to entry for providers and improves the inclusiveness and resilience of the system. Distributed computing networks reduce the cost of access for users by matching efficient computing resources through an open, competitive marketplace of providers, weakening the monopoly of centralized cloud providers.

HPChain is a computing network that provides accessible and cost-effective high-performance graphics processing unit (GPU) computing services through the use of a decentralized, peer-to-peer, “cloud + chain” protocol. Its modular blockchain infrastructure aims to reduce user costs and achieve flexible scalability to meet growing demand without sacrificing security or transparency in resource allocation.

The HPChain ecosystem currently includes an artificial intelligence cloud computing platform for GPU leasing, image creation, and algorithm sharing, and a cloud gaming platform that uses HPChain's GPU network to implement games on low-configuration devices. HPChain combines edge computing with competitive, transparent pricing to reduce latency. Its goal is to democratize affordable access to high-performance computing while enhancing the globally available GPU.

Other DePIN projects, such as [io.net](http://io.net), Akash Network, Render Network, and Aethir, are also leading scalable decentralized computing infrastructures. The demand for computing is increasing due to the great growth of artificial intelligence. However, with the emergence of many decentralized GPU protocols and the continued shortage of high-performance GPUs, such as A100 and H100, providers shift GPUs between computing networks in pursuit of the most lucrative token incentives. Inflationary pressures from token incentives can harm token holders. How to create differentiated services and retain consumers is what these GPU protocols need to think about. In addition, high-performance GPUs are in high demand and rarely have idle time. Therefore, the assumption of utilizing idle resources may not be feasible. The availability of computing power only during idle time makes decentralized computing performance unstable \[7\]. Stable performance is also a critical factor users consider other than cost.

##  6 Development trends of DePIN

Surfing the web on mobile devices has become the main way people use the web today. The exception is Web3, which is still in the early stages of development. However, smart entrepreneurs are already working on developing better mobile interfaces as mobile internet is irreversible. More and more users are gradually using mobile wallets of cryptocurrencies as it is more convenient for them to use when they cannot use their computers. This is what cryptocurrencies need to work on to become an important payment tool in everyday life. More powerful smartphones will also lead to further growth in mobile traffic. There will be more DePIN projects that allow users to interact with dApps from mobile devices. In order to cultivate user stickiness, Solana and Aptos blockchain launched their brand phones.

DePIN will drive electric vehicles to become the largest real-world application of Web3. According to OEC data ([https://oec.world/en/profile/hs/cars](https://oec.world/en/profile/hs/cars).), automobiles are the world's fourth largest trade product, with a total trade value of US$723 billion, accounting for 3.44% of the world's total trade in 2021. S&P Global Mobility \[8\] forecasts the 2024 global sales for battery electric passenger vehicles will grow to 13.3 million units, from 12% in 2023 to 16.2% market share. McKinsey \[9\] forecasts that global demand for electric vehicles will increase sixfold from 2021 to 2030, with annual sales rising from 6.5 million to about 40 million. Electric vehicles hold great promise as a future trend in the automotive industry. The convergence of cryptocurrencies, experiencing rapid growth in the virtual economy, with electric vehicles, a key driver in the real economy, is poised to gain recognition from mainstream investment entities and forward-thinking governments. This synergy is expected to receive significant support from crypto-native communities, collectively driving the development of both industries.

Although DePIN is a strong competitor to traditional infrastructure companies, they can co-exist and even cooperate to provide convenient services. After considering the costs and benefits, traditional infrastructure companies may not develop their business in rural or undeveloped regions. DePIN projects can perfectly match these market shares. DePin startups can use tokens to attract new users and use existing traditional infrastructure to achieve a win-win strategy.

##  7 Challenges of DePIN

While DePIN projects have promising prospects, they face some challenges in achieving widespread adoption.

Token incentives are necessary to facilitate bootstrapping and motivate participants to become distributed nodes. Physical equipment sales are an important source of revenue. If token rewards cannot cover costs or bring profits, users will not have the incentive to purchase hardware devices. Without network effects, the network cannot expand, causing the project to stall. However, excessive incentives can dilute the token's value for its holders. Token appreciation increases the burden on users who pay with tokens, potentially discouraging users from consuming if the quality of services is not worth it. This concern will result in a decline in token price. If tokens experience rapid, short-term fluctuations, it may affect the sustainable operation of the project. Most suppliers, consumers, and token holders join the network because of the wealth effect, so high-quality services are needed to keep the system sustainable. Balancing incentive marketing and holder interests requires teams to have skillful token economic design capabilities and excellent market makers to manage token prices appropriately. Some DePIN projects may issue multiple tokens within the ecosystem for synergy effects among different subDAOs. However, If the tokens of these subDAOs experience alternating increases and decreases in price over different time periods (for example, Token A increases while Token B decreases, and vice versa), it raises suspicion that the project may be engaging in market manipulation. This could involve the project's market makers using funds to manipulate the prices of tokens in subDAOs, potentially exploiting retail investors with limited financial experience through pump-and-dump schemes. DePIN's market makers have more control over the tokens, so there is a potential for moral hazard.

DePIN has significant growth potential but faces strong competition from industry giants in their respective fields. These large companies have well-established sales channels, advanced technological advantages, and strong government relationships, which make it difficult for DePIN projects to compete. Besides that, it is important to note that consumer habits favor existing products, making it even more challenging for DePIN to gain market share. These monopolies have gained their market share by beating off stiff competition from other traditional companies. Thus, it would be very difficult for the DePIN program to get a piece of the shares.

Markets in various regions have different operating rules, social cultures, and government mechanisms. The DePIN projects need to study local markets carefully before entering. Token reward activities may be sensitive and risky according to local laws. China's Ministry of State Security has issued a document stating that it will investigate people and companies collecting and stealing China's sensitive geospatial information data to prevent the illegal export of relevant data and eliminate the risk of leakage \[10\].

Cryptocurrencies have been quickly developing in recent years. With more than 420 million crypto users worldwide, global crypto ownership will reach an average of 4.2% in 2023 \[11\]. However, most people are still not familiar with the use of cryptocurrencies. There is an entry barrier for people to understand cryptocurrencies. Some people may consider cryptocurrencies as scams because they blur the distinction between genuine cryptocurrencies and scams that pretend to be valuable cryptocurrency investments but are pyramid schemes. The inefficiency and high cost of channels to exchange fiat currencies and cryptocurrencies are a barrier. Not to mention the difficulty of managing seed phrases well. Few cryptocurrencies have an interest in using DePIN, as most of them would only be attracted by potential investment opportunities. How to deploy and use DePIN products and ignite real demands may require startups to power more resources into education and promotions.

##  8 Summary

DePIN uses blockchain technology to provide transparency and cryptocurrencies to scale its network. DePIN represents the merging of virtual and physical economies. It is an important channel for educating the masses on the benefits of cryptocurrencies and improving society by offering cost-benefit services. By leveraging the financing function of cryptocurrencies, DePIN lowers the barrier to project initiation and is poised to transform various industries by improving existing products and services. DePIN could compete with existing industry giants or form complementary or collaborative partnerships. The smart design of the token economy and the quality of the service will be critical to the success of the DePIN projects. We expect DePIN projects to emerge and flourish in 2024 and 2025. However, whether DePIN projects are suitable for the real-world economy and can sustain long-term development remains to be observed over time.

# Chapter 5 DAO and DAO governance

1.  Qinxu Ding
2.  Weibiao Xu
3.  Zhiguo Wang
4.  School of Business, Singapore University of Social Sciences, Singapore, Singapore

## Abstract

Decentralized autonomous organizations (DAOs), short for decentralized autonomous organizations, represent a groundbreaking paradigm in organizational structure. Defined by smart contracts, and coded sets of rules governing their operation, DAOs automate tasks, facilitate coordination, and enable democratic decision-making without centralized leadership. This chapter conducts a systematic review of DAOs, encompassing their core principles, a proposed categorization framework, real-world applications, and an in-depth analysis of DAO governance, including voting systems and dispute resolution mechanisms.

## Keywords

Decentralized autonomous organizations (DAOs)

DAO governance

Dispute resolution

Voting schemes

##  1 Introduction of DAO

###  1.1 Definition of DAO

Decentralized autonomous organizations (DAOs) are organizations that allow individuals with shared goals to collaborate using blockchain infrastructure that enforces a set of shared rules. Typically, DAO members are registered, and each member has a unique address. Members can purchase any number of “governance tokens” associated with their addresses. These tokens are typically required to participate in the decision-making process. Decisions include determining how to use or allocate public resources within the DAO, such as funds or valuable assets.

The concept of a DAO lacks a universally accepted definition and remains a subject of ongoing debate \[1,2\]. Luis Cuende, co-founder of the Aragon DAO platform, defines it as “an internet-native entity with no central management which is regulated by a set of automatically enforceable rules on a public blockchain, and whose goal is to take a life of its own and incentivize people to achieve a shared common mission.” De Filippi and Hassan \[3\] state that in a DAO the interactive activities are mediated by a blockchain application. The application is governed by a set of rules written into its source code. According to De Filippi and Hassan \[4\], DAOs are ascribed the ability to hire people autonomously, provide services, gain money for their own aims, own smart property, coordinate with other autonomous software, or facilitate cooperation among various parties. Singh and Kim \[5\] define a DAO as an organization whose core functions are automated and that can agree, without human intervention, to the rules and principles specified in the code.

Unlike traditional firms with their centralized hierarchies and leadership structures, DAOs operate in a decentralized manner, with no CEOs or executives. Bound by smart contracts, all members have transparent access to operations and decision-making, a stark contrast to the often-opaque internal workings of conventional companies. Every change within a DAO requires member approval through a voting process, and its outcome is permanently etched onto the public blockchain. DAOs are powered by smart contracts, lines of code on a blockchain that act as their decentralized governing laws. These automated agreements handle tasks and decisions, allowing DAOs to function autonomously while hiring, servicing, and collaborating with other DAOs \[4,6\].

###  1.2 Common features of DAOs

Common features observed in many DAOs \[7,8\] can be categorized into the following three parts:

*   Self-operation: Imagine a DAO as a self-conducting orchestra, where smart contracts act as the invisible composer and conductor. Functions hum along on autopilot, decisions executed flawlessly without a single raised baton. Each instrument, representing a DAO member, plays its part, contributing to the harmonious whole. There's no maestro dictating the tune; the music flows from the collective code, a symphony of collaboration.
*   Self-governance: Members of DAOs hold voting rights and participate in making decisions that affect the network's direction and resource allocation. Specifically, in a DAO, hierarchy dissolves and is replaced by a level playing field of connected nodes. Each member holds a vote and a voice in shaping the organization's direction. Smart contracts become the rulebook, etched in lines of code, but not set in stone. Members can propose and pass amendments through votes, ensuring the DAO remains flexible and responsive to its community's needs. It is a dynamic tapestry woven by the collective will, constantly adapting to its environment.
*   Self-coordination: Distributed networks in DAOs work together seamlessly, synchronizing actions and information without a central hub or intermediary. In a DAO, where every action hinges on preprogrammed rules, aligning participant responsibilities and management structure is crucial. Think of it as building a well-oiled machine: each part needs to function seamlessly together for the DAO to thrive.

###  1.3 Categorizations and types of DAOs

Research on DAOs is still in its early stages, but attempts to categorize these novel organizational structures are crucial for understanding their potential and challenges. This chapter proposes a three-pronged approach for DAO classification, each offering unique insights:

*   By origins: Native Custom DAOs: These organizations, exemplified by “The DAO” (2016) and MakerDAO (2017), are built from the ground up with custom smart contracts. Domain experts often design and manage these DAOs, leveraging their specialized knowledge to facilitate complex functionalities like decentralized finance (DeFi) in MakerDAO's case.
*   By deployment platform: DAO-as-a-Service Platforms: Recognizing the technical barriers to DAO creation, platforms like Aragon, DAOstack, DAOhaus, and Colony emerged. These platforms offer prebuilt infrastructure and customizable templates, enabling individuals without deep blockchain expertise to establish and govern their own DAOs.
*   By objective: Objective-Based Categorization: This approach focuses on the underlying purpose of a DAO, classifying them based on their goals. For example, some DAOs might prioritize investment and fundraising, while others may be driven by community governance or social impact initiatives.

##  2 DAO governance

###  2.1 Definition of DAO governance

The academic literature (e.g., \[9–13\]) presents a mosaic of perspectives on their governance structures. Early notions, such as Williamson's \[14\] focus on “good order and effective arrangements,” were later refined by Introna \[15\] to encompass “a code of conduct for independent actors who lack unilateral decision-making power.” Building upon these foundations, this chapter proposes a definition of DAO governance as a distributed system of rules encoded in blockchain-based smart contracts. These rules establish collective decision-making mechanisms and guide the self-management and coordination of the organization's activities, eliminating the need for centralized authority. This system empowers DAO members through governance tokens, which grant them voting rights on proposals for strategic and operational changes.

###  2.2 General governance framework

####  2.2.1 Agenda setting

In the corporate setting, the board of directors convenes to determine the eligibility of proposals for shareholder voting, essentially setting the agenda for significant decisions. This selected group of decision-makers serves as gatekeepers, responsible for both proposing and deciding which matters make it onto the agenda. This approach has its merits and drawbacks. On the positive side, a small group can swiftly reach a consensus, minimizing the potential for abuse with numerous low-quality proposals \[7\]. However, the concentration of power is a downside, as not all shareholders are granted the ability to propose agenda items for voting, raising questions about whether the board consistently acts in the shareholders’ best interests.

In contrast, within the context of DAOs, allowing all governance token holders to immediately propose items for voting poses its own set of challenges. Without an effective barrier or filter to assess proposals beforehand, an overwhelming number of unchecked proposals could burden voters. In the decentralized realm, even with prevetting, motivating sufficient voter engagement is already challenging \[16\], making this a substantial concern. This issue could escalate if a malicious actor inundates the system with numerous proposals, akin to spam emails, given the minimal effort and cost involved in submission. Another issue pertains to token holders lacking the necessary knowledge or expertise to make informed votes on specific proposals. Additionally, proposers may not invest sufficient effort in researching an issue before submitting a proposal, potentially diminishing the proposal's quality. A more significant concern involves individual token holders proposing with self-interest rather than the best interests of the DAO's objectives. Considering these highlighted issues, making proposals immediately available for voting could lead to a squandering of limited resources \[17\].

Determining the proposals eligible for voting holds critical significance for DAOs, and decentralized mechanisms can address the outlined issues in this regard. Two types of agenda-setting mechanisms can be considered.

To curb the submission of an excessive number of proposals, DAOs may institute a cost for proposal submission, where submitters are required to pay a fee in tokens for each new proposal. For instance, Dash DAO charges five tokens (USD 70.18 per token as of February 26, 2023). Some DAOs also mandate proposers to stake tokens for the proposal's duration, such as Uniswap, which requires 10 million votes for an on-chain proposal. These fees and staking requirements act as barriers to deter frivolous and harmful proposals although ongoing debates question their impact on those genuinely wishing to propose significant changes but lacking sufficient tokens. To address this concern, refunding the fee for approved proposals can be considered, with the proposer suggesting the refund amount in their proposal. However, this approach requires small token holders to possess an adequate number of tokens to participate. Moreover, the proposal fee need not be uniform and can vary based on the nature and value of the proposal \[18\].

Another strategy to mitigate excessive proposal submissions is to restrict access based on reputation. Members can earn a reputation by contributing to the DAO ecosystem, such as voting in line with the majority, putting forward winning proposals, or maintaining recent participation, as seen in DAOstack and Colony. Unlike tokens, reputation is nontransferable, discouraging the splitting of reputation across multiple accounts. Concentrating reputation in a single wallet serves to prevent members from inundating the system with proposals through multiple accounts and enhances the power of a singular account.

####  2.2.2 Voter eligibility

The framework for evaluating voting schemes in DAO governance should encompass various aspects. The initial segment of this framework comprises two dimensions. The first dimension, voting eligibility, outlines the criteria for identifying entities eligible for voting power, with three distinct criteria types: one token, one vote, one person, one vote, and restricted voting.

In the one, token, one, vote model, each token held by a DAO member in a single wallet represents one vote. This approach may lead to centralized voting power, with a few major holders commanding a majority of votes. The one person, one vote model restricts voting to one vote per wallet; however, the openness and anonymity of current blockchain systems allow token holders to create multiple wallets, potentially bypassing this criterion. Restricted voting, the third model, confines voting to specific members, such as those with a minimum number of governance tokens or reputation holders.

While limiting the pool of eligible voters might seem contrary to decentralization principles, restrictive voting systems are implemented to enhance the decision-making process. Various types of restricted voting exist, contingent on the identity of the restricted voters.

Members enjoy voting rights contingent upon specific eligibility criteria, including holding a minimum quantity of tokens or staking a predetermined sum of cryptocurrency within the DApp. Alternatively, reputation holders have voting rights limited to those possessing a designated level of reputation, earned through contributions to the DAO community, typically in governance or project-related endeavors. Governance token holders, a subset of the DAO community, possess exclusive voting rights, specifically tied to a particular governance token, which may differ from the primary token of the DAO. Another facet involves delegation, a mechanism within the governance token holder category, allowing token holders to delegate their voting authority to another member. This approach facilitates more efficient and effective decision-making, empowering token holders who lack the time or expertise for active governance participation to still influence the protocol's future direction passively.

####  2.2.3 The voting process

The voting process in a DAO is similar to a shareholder meeting, where all eligible voters gather together to vote on a single proposal at hand. In a DAO, each voter has one vote. Once a vote is recorded permanently on the blockchain, it cannot be reversed.

One of the advantages of blockchain-based DAOs is that proposals and their voting results can be inspected by others on the spot. However, a disadvantage is that not all eligible voters are able to participate in the process, leading to low voter turnout.

####  2.2.4 Incentive mechanisms

DAO management requires incentive mechanisms. Because everyone is independent, in the absence of centralized management, everyone is for their own interests to maintain the management of DAO, which is not conducive to the sustainable development of DAO. Here we discuss some incentive mechanisms/tools.

Incentivizing voter participation in DAOs involves various approaches. One method ties the prize size to the number of votes, providing greater rewards for increased participation, although this could discourage those with fewer tokens. Another strategy introduces a random lucky draw, offering an equal chance of winning to all voters regardless of their token wealth, but it may attract participants solely interested in prizes and risks multiple account creation. The deposit-based reward model, proposed by Dfinity, requires voters to deposit tokens with a 3-month withdrawal restriction, and rewards are determined by the deposited tokens and the number of voted proposals. Beyond tokens, reputation awards are introduced, wherein active voters receive reputation credits, correlating with higher voting power.

Addressing motivational challenges, a loss aversion model penalizes token holders with losses if they abstain from voting \[19\]. Additionally, a governance token separation approach rewards voters with a distinct governance token, exemplified by MakerDAO's DAI and MKR tokens, allowing for a clear division of utility and governance rights.

####  2.2.5 The consensus mechanism

To reach a consensus on voting results, DAOs need to consider two features. The first is the passing standard for proposals. There are some existing commonly used standards. The most straightforward standard is a simple majority approval. Specifically, voters will cast a “yes,” “no,” or “abstain” vote on a particular proposal. The category with the highest vote share will determine the voting result. In addition, a supermajority can be added on top of a simple majority. Any given proposal's passage requires a minimum percentage of “yes” votes to reach an absolute majority. For example, the Dash DAO requires at least 10% of the master nodes to vote “yes” on a proposal for it to pass. The second feature is based on a minimum voting rate, called quorum voting. Quorum voting requires voting participation to be no less than a certain threshold (such as 50% or 60%). If the quorum is not reached, the proposal will automatically be rejected \[1,2\].

####  2.2.6 Voting schemes

In the world of DAOs, there are eight different voting schemes prevailing: token-based quorum voting, quadratic voting, weighted voting (or reputation-based voting), knowledge-extractable voting, multisig voting, holographic consensus, conviction voting, and rage quitting voting \[1,2\]. [Table 1](#Ch005_61-66_B9780443347177000192.xhtml#t0010) shows the summary of these schemes.

[Table 1](#Ch005_61-66_B9780443347177000192.xhtml#B-t0010)

A brief overview of different voting schemes.

 
| Voting schemes || Description || Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Token-based quorum voting || Quorum voting is a commonly used mechanism in DAO governance. For any given proposal, the participating voters in the voting process must exceed the certain preset threshold (e.g., 50% or 60%) of the total voters, or else, the proposal will automatically be rejected || KyberDAO and Aave |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Quadratic voting || Quadratic voting allows voters to express the intensity of their preferences by allocating multiple units of voting power to a single proposal. The need for higher voting power is increased by the square of the number of tokens || Gitcoin and BrightID |
| Weighted voting (reputation-based voting) || Weighted voting refers to a voting system where each voter has a certain number of votes they can cast, and the weight of each vote is determined by the number of votes a voter has. This means that a voter with more votes has a greater influence on the outcome of the vote compared to a voter with fewer votes || BPC DAO and OrangeDAO |
| Knowledge-extractable voting || Knowledge-extractable voting is a type of voting system in which the knowledge or expertise of voters is considered when determining the outcome of a vote. This can be done by allowing voters to indicate their level of expertise on a given subject or by using algorithms to assess the quality of their contributions to a discussion or debate || DIT Protocol |
| Multisig voting || Multisig voting is a voting mechanism where multiple signatures or approvals are required before a proposal can be executed. It is typically used as a security measure to ensure that a certain level of consensus is reached before any action is taken on the blockchain || Gnosis Safe, Aragon Client DAOs, and BitDAO |
| Holographic consensus || Holographic consensus is a voting mechanism intended to filter relevant proposals for large communities. A small group of voters will make decisions on behalf of the majority, but the proposal could be selected by the market participant with incentive designs || DXdao, necDAO, and DAOstack |
| Conviction voting || Conviction voting is a voting system in which members of the community can vote on proposals by staking their tokens for a certain period of time. The longer the stake period, the more “conviction” a member has in their vote and the more weight their vote carries || Giveth, Common Stack, and MetaCartel |
| Rage quitting voting || Rage quitting voting refers to the voting mechanism where a token holder, who is unhappy with the outcome of a vote or the direction of the organization, can withdraw their stake and sell their tokens, rather than continuing to support the organization || MetaCartel Ventures, MolochDAO, and DAOhaus |

There may be other voting scheme concepts as well, for example, liquid voting, also known as proxy voting. The idea behind liquid voting is to align the interests of token holders with the interests of the DAO. By giving token holders more voting power based on the number of tokens they hold, the system incentivizes them to hold tokens and participate in the DAO, rather than selling them. This helps ensure that the long-term health and success of the DAO are aligned with the interests of its token holders.

The choice of a voting scheme is an important decision for any DAO. The best scheme for a particular DAO will depend on a number of factors, including the size and complexity of the DAO, the desired level of participation, and the risk of governance attacks.

####  2.2.7 Dispute resolution

In principle, the atomic settlement of smart contracts that empower DAOs is expected to diminish the risk of disputes. Nevertheless, it is imperative to acknowledge that the complete elimination of dispute risk is unattainable \[7\]. The presence of flawed code within smart contracts can lead to economic detriment affecting either the entirety or individual members of the DAO. Furthermore, these smart contracts may prove inadequate in meeting the evolving needs of the DAO in the future, a concern heightened in emergency situations where disputes among DAO members are likely to emerge.

On the other hand, when selecting a dispute resolution mechanism, it is imperative to assess factors such as cost and its applicability to both high- and low-value claims.

An effective dispute resolution method should also prioritize time efficiency. Given that DAO members often originate from diverse jurisdictions, it is essential that the chosen method demonstrates effectiveness across various legal landscapes. Disputes within DAOs frequently necessitate specialized subject matter expertise, particularly in areas such as the coding of smart contracts and legal intricacies. The absence of this combined knowledge may pose challenges in the resolution of disputes. Moreover, complicating matters, DAO members often maintain anonymity. Even if a dispute resolution mechanism is theoretically robust, its enforcement may prove challenging if reliant on the disclosure of parties’ identities \[7\].

Existing dispute resolution methods like courts or tribunals may not be suitable for DAO disputes based on the above factors. To overcome this problem, Decentralized Dispute Resolution Services (DDRS) are recently proposed \[20\]. DDRS functions akin to a “digital court,” utilizing blockchain technology, engaging a jury sourced from the crowd, and incorporating economic incentives to ensure equitable rulings. Upon the emergence of a dispute within a DAO, a random selection of jurors is chosen from a pool of token holders who have staked their tokens as collateral. This group of jurors assumes the responsibility of determining the dispute's resolution. In the event that one or both disputing parties dissent from the outcome, they have the option to file an appeal at a higher court, albeit incurring a substantial cost. Jurors aligning their votes with the majority decision receive a reward, while those dissenting face penalties, including the slashing of their staked tokens.

DDRS employs the Schelling point mechanism, which relies on the expectation that individuals, anticipating honest voting by others, will themselves be incentivized to vote truthfully to align with the majority. This shared anticipation of honesty fosters a reliance on others to vote in good faith. Representing a new generation of online dispute resolution (ODR) built on blockchain, DDRS utilizes smart contracts to enforce the outcomes of dispute resolution. Remarkably, DDRS can operate without knowledge of the parties’ identities, requiring only their public keys. Well-known examples of DDRS include Keros ([https://kleros.io/](https://kleros.io/)) and Aragon Court ([https://github.com/aragon/aragon-court](https://github.com/aragon/aragon-court)).

However, there are also limitations of DDRS. Presently, the majority of the aforementioned DDRS methods are predominantly applicable to binary cases—instances characterized by only two potential outcomes in a dispute. For instance, one may choose either approve or reject a proposal. However, real disputes often exhibit greater complexity, rendering them unable to be accurately represented through binary categorization. This limitation poses a significant constraint on the efficacy of DDRS in addressing more intricate and multifaceted dispute scenarios.

##  3 Conclusion

In conclusion, this chapter has delved into the realm of DAOs, shedding light on various facets of DAO governance, encompassing voting mechanisms and dispute resolution methods. The objective has been to furnish a valuable overview and point of reference for researchers and industry practitioners seeking a thorough exploration of this field.

As we look ahead, numerous avenues for future research emerge. A compelling direction involves conducting an exhaustive analysis of the delegation's role within the framework of DAO governance, exploring its influence on token prices, and scrutinizing its incentive structures. These lines of inquiry present just a glimpse of the potential research questions that can enhance our understanding of DAOs and anticipate their evolving dynamics. The journey of exploration and discovery in this domain is far from over, and these forthcoming inquiries promise to contribute significantly to the ongoing discourse surrounding decentralized autonomous organizations.
