# Chapter 22 Application of blockchain and internet of things in ESG data platforms

1.  Nguyen Huynh Long Hung
2.  Alan Megargel
3.  School of Computing and Information Systems, Singapore Management University, Singapore, Singapore

## Abstract

Sustainable finance refers to the channeling of capital toward environmental, social, and governance (ESG) purposes. As of December 2022, the global market value of sustainable financing is estimated to be US$3.7 trillion. The lack of high-quality, standardized, and trusted ESG data is a major challenge in promoting sustainable finance. With the aim of overcoming this challenge, our paper first reviews previous work done on the use of blockchain technologies and internet of things (IoT) as applied to ESG data platforms. Next, we examine three large ESG data platform projects, namely Project Greenprint, Project Benja, and Project Genesis, which have implemented blockchain and IoT. In doing so, we provide a comprehensive view of how blockchain technology and IoT could be incorporated into the design and enhancement of such platforms. Our paper aims to provide guidelines for academic researchers and industry practitioners on how to apply blockchain technology and IoT to build an ESG data platform that can be used to support the development of sustainable finance markets.

## Keywords

Blockchain

Internet of things

Data platform

Environmental

Social

Governance

Sustainable financing

##  1 Introduction

There has been an increase in attention given to environmental, social, and governance (ESG) issues in recent years. It has become a key agenda item for government agencies, corporations, investors, and the academic community. A broad definition of ESG or environmental social responsibility is that it seeks to address a wide range of issues, from the reduction of greenhouse gases to the promotion of renewable energy sources, as well as ensuring gender equality, product safety, and stakeholder rights among others. Sustainable finance refers to the process of taking ESG considerations into account when making financing decisions, with the aim of fostering long-term investment in sustainable economic activities. Originally emerging as a focus of a small group of investors, sustainable finance (aka ESG finance) has gradually become a mainstream investment theme for asset managers \[1\]. The growth of assets under management that incorporate ESG factors has grown exponentially over the past decade. In the United States, the level of ESG investing in 2018 was over 20% of all professionally managed assets, at over US$11 trillion (Singapore International Foundation, [www.sif.org.sg](http://www.sif.org.sg)). In Europe, that number was over US$17 trillion. Climate Bonds says sustainable finance is on its way to being a US$5 trillion market in the latter half of this decade. It is growing at a Compound Annual Growth Rate (CAGR) of around 22.4% between 2023 and 2032 \[2\].

The lack of high-quality standardized ESG data on companies, especially in Asia, is a major challenge to unlocking capital for the region's transition to green economies and sustainable societies. The collection of ESG data is mostly performed manually, which is tedious and prone to error. The lack of data, which is a common problem for Small and Medium-sized Enterprises (SMEs), can limit further analytics in terms of ESG ratings and monitoring. This happens because SMEs usually do not have sufficient resources to produce all necessary ESG data required by mainstream ESG frameworks. ESG reports lack transparency, reducing credibility and posing risks of greenwashing (the process of conveying a false message that a company's products are environmentally friendly). ESG rating agencies, investors, and financial institutions primarily assess companies based on their ESG self-disclosure reports, whose authenticity can be challenged. Listed companies are reluctant to share their own data with external parties, especially their competitors. Data privacy and trade secrets require reliable systems to guarantee confidentiality for sharing. These disadvantages in the ESG data value chain can potentially be solved using digital technologies, such as Blockchain and the internet of things (IoT).

It is possible for smaller businesses and individuals to participate in the market of sustainable finance by tokenizing carbon credits (an application of blockchain technology) in a way that allows fractional ownership of carbon credits. Finally, an ESG data platform on which all relevant stakeholders linked to the ESG data journey can interact with one another is another proposition that has the potential to contribute to the growth of a seamless sustainable finance ecosystem. The purpose of this one-stop-shop platform is to provide participants with an easy, transparent, and automated way to disclose ESG-related information and get verified, rated, and funded in an efficient and transparent way.

##  2 Blockchain application in ESG

Blockchain is a distributed ledger of immutable, cryptographically secured timestamped records \[3\]. It is based on a peer-to-peer network where participants can independently verify each other's transactions without a centralized party \[4\]. Blockchain also empowers smart contracts, computer programs that allow a procedure to be automatically executed per predefined conditions.

Blockchain types are classified based on read-write access to the distributed ledger, validation rights, and consensus algorithm. In a public (permissionless) blockchain, every node has an equal read access to the ledger, while the right is restricted to some limited members for private (permissioned) blockchains. In the permissioned blockchain, only certain members have write access and participate in the consensus, while any node can perform these tasks in the permissionless blockchain. As there is generally no mining process required in permissioned blockchains, faster throughputs, and higher volumes can be achieved, with consensus finality being also guaranteed.

Blockchain-based circular economy ideas for the built environment were put forth by Shojaei et al. \[5\]. The materials needed to make a product are tracked in this case using a blockchain strategy. The suggested approach offers reusable options that lower the environmental pollution rate.

Agrawal et al. \[6\] showed that blockchain could contribute to enhancing ESG factors of supply chain. Ko et al. \[7\] compared two competitors in manufacturing, and one of them deployed blockchain to ensure financial transparency and establish trust between business partners. The results suggested this blockchain-leveraged firm improved profitability and competitiveness. Venkatesh et al. \[8\] designed a system architecture that integrated blockchain, IoT, and big data analytics to allow companies to monitor their supply chain social sustainability efficiently and effectively.

Liu et al. \[9\] proposed a blockchain-based workflow for ESG assessment using both on-chain and off-chain approaches, illustrated in [Fig. 1](#Ch022_321-333_B978044334717700009X.xhtml#f0010). In the off-chain part, listed companies upload ESG data and reports into the blockchain in the ESG reporting stage. Subsequently, the on-chain will act as a transparent and immutable ledger that further cascades ESG data to other stakeholders.

![Fig. 1 Blockchain-based workflow for ESG.](images/B978044334717700009X/f22-01-9780443347177.jpg)

[Fig. 1](#Ch022_321-333_B978044334717700009X.xhtml#B-f0010) Blockchain-based workflow for ESG.

The diagram shows the process starting with listed companies providing E S G data through E S G reporting. This data is then used by E S G rating agencies such as F T S E 4 Good, M S C I, Refinitiv, Sustainalytics, Vigeo Eiris and C D P for E S G assessment. The steps in E S G assessment include acquiring data, standardizing data, evaluating using S M A A-2 and calculating and publishing the score. The E S G data and score are then processed through a blockchain and shared with other stakeholders like the H K Exchange and investors.

The data integrity that blockchain can offer, which is essential from a sustainability perspective, is frequently praised \[10\]. With the introduction of digital measurement reporting and verification, data supply chains are becoming more and more significant, especially in the voluntary carbon markets, where accurate monitoring is required to ensure real carbon reductions. Ex-post proof of offsets is becoming more and more necessary, and blockchain-enabled data supply chains can offer data assurance, integrity, and audibility.

The financing and trading of unlisted securities may be completely transformed by blockchain technology, particularly by tokenization. Blockchain technology has the potential to speed up and simplify transactions. It can be applied to all asset classes, including those that are ESG-driven, like shares or bonds issued by businesses that produce solar energy.

The concept of tokenization is the transfer of ownership rights (such as equity, bonds, real estate, etc.) of an asset into a digital token, for the asset to be used. Blockchain ecosystems make it possible to transfer, store, and verify data and value contained within tokens in an efficient and secure manner.

Purchasing a financial asset (such as shares or a bond) nowadays involves several processes. Consequently, Delivery Versus Payment (DvP) can take up to four business days, depending on the type of asset. By contrast, tokenization could make the DvP process easier and faster. Assets can be transferred at any time, and even a fractionalised amount. That creates the potential for better liquidity and easier and cheaper trading. By structuring an asset's data, whether it is project data, financial data, or ESG data, into a single data source through tokenization, we can standardize and simplify the various due diligence processes (technical, financial, ESG, and legal).

##  3 IoT application in ESG

IoT is “the network of physical objects that are embedded with sensors, software, and other technologies for the purpose of connecting and exchanging data with other devices and systems over the internet” \[11\]. The objects can either be sensors that detect physical signals in the environment (light, humidity, touch, gas, etc.) or actuators that convert electronic signals into physical movements (such as rotary motors). Data collected from these sensors (dispatched to actuators) will be transferred through different communication protocols, depending on design and capacity, Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE), Bluetooth 5, Zigbee, Long Range (LoRa), Wireless Fidelity (Wi-Fi), Narrowband-IoT (NB-IoT), Sigfox, Advanced Message Queuing Protocol (AMQP), Data Distribution Service (DDS), Message Queue Telemetry Transport (MQTT), etc. [Fig. 2](#Ch022_321-333_B978044334717700009X.xhtml#f0015) illustrates an IoT-based architecture for ESG.

![Fig. 2 IoT-based architecture for ESG.](images/B978044334717700009X/f22-02-9780443347177.jpg)

[Fig. 2](#Ch022_321-333_B978044334717700009X.xhtml#B-f0015) IoT-based architecture for ESG.

The diagram shows three main components: Environment Report, Social Report and Governance Report. Each of these components collects data through I o T sensors. The Environment Report collects environmental data through I o T sensors, the Social Report collects social data through I o T sensors and the Governance Report collects governance data through I o T sensors. These data are transmitted via Zigbee, L o R a, Bluetooth, 3G, 4G, 5G and Wi-Fi to an I o T-based Gateway. The I o T-based Gateway then communicates with a Cloud Server using M Q T T, A M Q P, T C P and I P protocols. Finally, the Cloud Server generates an E S G Report through an API.

IoT can greatly assist companies in monitoring and measuring their ESG performance. Through sensors, ESG data can be accurately captured in a timely manner, and then presented meaningfully to relevant stakeholders. Many companies today are using IoT to support their ESG reporting by monitoring water usage, carbon emissions, etc.

An edge computing and IoT-based supply chain management system were proposed by Wang et al. \[12\] and followed up by Saxena et al. \[13\]. Edge computing is used to provide the supply chain management system with appropriate data processing and analysis services. The supply chain management system's cost and risk are reduced through the implementation of IoT. Shared and connected data are used to create the best possible set of data for subsequent processes. The main purpose of the suggested method is to increase the system's efficiency and reliability.

Most standard approaches to ensure IoT security and privacy are primarily managed centrally, leading to limited scalability and trust issues. This necessitates a decentralization approach using blockchain in which authenticity and immutability can be enhanced. Furthermore, blockchain can promote an IoT ecosystem of services and data marketplaces by leveraging microservices in a trustless environment \[14\].

An industry 4.0 supply chain management system built on blockchain was introduced by Esmaeilian et al. \[15\]. The study employs IoT to deliver essential business services. Sector development rates are accelerated by the IoT, which increases efficiency. By encouraging customers to adopt environmentally friendly habits, blockchain technology helps to lower environmental pollution. The system's performance is improved as a result of the blockchain's ability to lower development costs and increase operational efficiency.

In integrating blockchain with IoT, Reyna et al. \[14\] provided a comparison of three designs: IoT-IoT (IoT devices communicating with each other directly, leaving only some data stored in blockchain), IoT-Blockchain (all interactions going through blockchain), and hybrid approach (mixed use of the two former designs). The first approach provides the lowest latency, but reliable IoT data exchange is required. The second approach ensures all transactions are securely recorded, but at the expense of more bandwidth needed. The hybrid approach, when combined with “FOG” (cloud-like properties, but closer to the “ground,” i.e., IoT devices) edge computing, can potentially enhance the performance of blockchain and the IoT network. All three approaches are illustrated in [Fig. 3](#Ch022_321-333_B978044334717700009X.xhtml#f0020).

![Fig. 3 IoT-Blockchain integration design.](images/B978044334717700009X/f22-03-9780443347177.jpg)

[Fig. 3](#Ch022_321-333_B978044334717700009X.xhtml#B-f0020) IoT-Blockchain integration design.

All three approaches are illustrated. The first approach, I o T-I o T, shows a connection between a phone, a computer and a car, all linked to a central node. The second approach, I o T-Blockchain, depicts a similar setup with a phone, a computer and a car, but the connections are shown with dashed lines. The third approach, Hybrid approach, includes a phone, a computer, a car and an additional component labeled F O G, which is connected to a cloud. The connections in this approach are a mix of solid and dashed lines.

##  4 ESG data platform

Investors play a catalyst role in pressuring companies to adopt ESG metrics in their corporate strategies. To assess how sustainable their portfolio companies are, investors, asset managers, and financial institutions need high-quality quantitative and qualitative ESG data \[16\], currently offered by ESG rating agencies like Sustainalytics and Morgan Stanley Capital International (MSCI). Companies disclose ESG data on the platform per regulators’ requests and seek investors’ funding in the same venue. To comply with covenants and Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) typically set in ESG financing products, companies potentially will have to disclose ESG data of their suppliers as well (such as the Scope 3 greenhouse gases measurement). The ESG data platform can also provide companies with insights into their ESG practices and help them align with sustainability goals. Regulators use ESG ratings and information to monitor and enforce compliance with sustainability regulations. ESG rating providers assess companies’ ESG disclosure per global reporting frameworks such as Taskforce on Climate-Related Financial Disclosures (TCFD), Sustainability Accounting Standards Board (SASB), Global Reporting Initiative (GRI), Carbon Disclosure Project (CDP), and Global Real Estate Sustainability Benchmark (GRESB), then finalize an assessment score for financing purposes. According to a recent study by Inmarsat, in which they surveyed more than 1000 senior technology and ESG professionals with sustainability decision-making power, 76% of the respondents do not trust their peers’ ESG reporting, suggesting a single source of truth is essential to back up these sustainability claims \[17\]. That necessitates the ESG data providers whose role is to collect raw data at sources using IoT sensors, upstreaming to the platform via other data aggregators. The platform may include other participants who bring added utilities, such as data analytics functions to assist investors with making sound investment decisions.

Currently, there is a rising number of green technology companies in the market that provide solutions for one or multiple stages in the ESG data journey: from data acquisition to data aggregation and analytics. Hitachi has been developing a proprietary Sustainable Finance Platform, illustrated in [Fig. 4](#Ch022_321-333_B978044334717700009X.xhtml#f0025), using IoT and blockchain technologies to improve the visibility and verification of environmental projects \[18\].

![Fig. 4 Hitachi's sustainable finance ecosystem.](images/B978044334717700009X/f22-04-9780443347177.jpg)

[Fig. 4](#Ch022_321-333_B978044334717700009X.xhtml#B-f0025) Hitachi's sustainable finance ecosystem.

A cyclic infographic illustrating the components of Sustainable Finance. The central component is labeled 'Sustainable Finance'. Surrounding it are the following components: 'Green Bond Issuer', 'External Reviewer', 'Project Owner', 'Service Company', 'Underwriter' and 'Investor'. Additional labels include 'Efficient Reporting', 'Aggregation', 'Enhanced Decision-Making' and 'Green Assets Transparent & Secure'.

There are also some government-led projects in trial, in which they attempt to build a unified ESG ecosystem that connects all these stakeholders for efficiency, such as Project Genesis led by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA), and Project Greenprint led by the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS).

In essence, an ESG data platform would need the consumers of ESG data (investors, banks, etc.), data providers who are companies and other data acquirers, the monitors who are regulatory bodies, auditors and rating agencies, and the data orchestrators who act as the middlemen to facilitate the flow of ESG data.

##  5 Project greenprint

To harness technology and data to enable a more transparent, trusted, and efficient ESG ecosystem to promote green and sustainable finance, MAS has launched Project Greenprint—a collaborative effort with the financial services industry. The project aims to “grow a vibrant Green FinTech ecosystem in Singapore and scaling Green FinTech solutions beyond Singapore; enable connections across financial institutions, investors, green technology and solution providers, ESG service providers, and corporates; develop digital infrastructure to facilitate the flow of consistent, clear and reliable ESG data, with access to other global and sectoral data platforms” \[19\]. The proposed ecosystem is a collection of four platform components described as follows and illustrated in [Fig. 5](#Ch022_321-333_B978044334717700009X.xhtml#f0030).

1.  1. **ESG Disclosure Portal:** An integrated portal that supports companies in their ESG disclosure journey beginning from data reporting for regulatory compliance, fostering best practices via industry benchmarking and ultimately meeting investor needs for a consistent and reliable source of ESG data. Titled “ESGenome,” the ESG Disclosure Portal was developed by SGX (Singapore Exchange) and currently hosts Singapore-listed companies during their pilot phase.
2.  2. **ESG Registry:** ESGpedia, developed in partnership with Hashstacs Pte Ltd. (“STACS”), draws on a blockchain solution to record and maintain the provenance of green certifications issued by various sectoral bodies. It allows banks to access green certifications issued by various bodies for their green and sustainable financing decisions.
3.  3. **Data Orchestrator** aims to aggregate ESG data from multiple data sources. This will include major ESG data providers, utility providers, sectoral platforms, and of course the ESG Data Registry. The Data Orchestrator will provide consent-based access to these sources. It will also allow new data insights to be generated through data analytics to better support investment and financing decisions.
4.  4. **Marketplace** aims to connect ESG technology providers to investors, financial institutions, and corporates, to facilitate partnerships and investments for ESG solutions.

![Fig. 5 Project Greenprint.](images/B978044334717700009X/f22-05-9780443347177.jpg)

[Fig. 5](#Ch022_321-333_B978044334717700009X.xhtml#B-f0030) Project Greenprint.

The proposed ecosystem is a collection of four platform components described as follows and illustrated in Fig. 5. The components are: Greenprint Marketplace, E S G Disclosure Portal, Data Orchestrator(s) and E S G Registry(s). The Greenprint Marketplace is connected to E S G Disclosure Portal, Data Orchestrator(s) and E S G Registry(s). The E S G Disclosure Portal is connected to E S G data providers. The Data Orchestrator(s) is connected to E S G data providers, Common Utilities and Open Data (Satellite, Nature). The E S G Registry(s) is connected to Sectoral Systems and Sectoral Certifications.

It is worth mentioning that ESGpedia draws on a blockchain solution to record and maintain the provenance of green certifications issued by various sectoral bodies (agriculture, transport, construction, etc.). In addition, sectoral data providers, such as CO2 Connect (CO2X), can leverage IoT technology to acquire and upstream real-time data to data orchestrators for further cascade in the ecosystem.

Using CO2X's data tracking and analytics capabilities, Singlife publishes sustainability reports for its policyholders on ESGpedia. By assessing and monitoring the environmental impact and costs of new motor insurance policies with this information obtained with the consent of insurance policyholders, Singlife will be able to efficiently develop and better structure new motor insurance policies. Fuel consumption, carbon emissions, and carbon intensity are among the data collected by ESGpedia. In addition, it provides benchmarking against industry standards, as well as overall carbon savings levels, which enhances visibility for companies looking to track their sustainability performance. As a result, financial institutions will also have access to this data and can use it to formulate data-driven strategies to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. This initiative involves Singlife insuring a fleet of electric vehicles on behalf of EVFY Pte Ltd. ([www.evfy.sg](http://www.evfy.sg)), an environmentally friendly logistic company and customer of the CO2X platform. To expand its motor insurance offering to other electric vehicle fleet operators, Singlife will assess all collected carbon data and monthly emissions reports independently.

##  6 Project Benja

In the typical bond product lifecycle, there are three major components: primary market operations (issuing, subscription, and distribution), secondary market activities (trading, clearing, and settlement), and post-trade tasks (processing, custody, and asset servicing). The inefficiency is frequently observed at the stages of issuance, distribution, and post-trade asset servicing, and is particularly evident at the issuance and distribution stages. There are a variety of requirements that go along with an ordinary bond offering, and the process can take anywhere from a few weeks to many months. As a first step toward addressing the problems present in the bond market now, Project Benja was established to assist with facilitating bond issuances more easily, as well as improving operational efficiency throughout the entire lifecycle of bonds, particularly during the origination stage and the post-trade stage of bond issuance. STACS was the project manager as well as the partner for the distributed ledger technology (DLT) solution for this project.

To address the capital markets in a practical and sustainable manner, Project Benja was established by STACS in collaboration with Deutsche Bank Securities Services. It is Project Benja's goal to harness smart contracts to develop an end-to-end flow of work, which encompasses ESG bonds and the formulation of social-inclusivity formats to leverage smart contracts. Two of the key elements that are essential to the management of ESG bonds are real-time impact reporting on-chain as well as an immutable and transparent management of proceeds management.

ESG standards are programmed into security tokens according to the bond parameters and green elements that are needed. As a result of the automation gains, smaller units and minimum lot sizes can be included in the product range. The eligibility requirements for subscriptions and the mandate of ESG investments are enforced with the help of smart contracts, which provide efficient settlements for DvPs. The proceeds of the transaction can be programmed to be sent only to green-certified parties, if smart contracts are used to enforce this. On the blockchain, proceeds are managed and transparent in terms of their use. The scalability of asset servicing across a wide range of markets is also a benefit of automatic interest payment and principal redemption to lower costs of operation. If the green sustainable KPIs are exceeded, then financial incentives (e.g., lower coupon rates) can be programmed into the smart contract as additional incentives. When connected to data sources, greenwashing can be prevented since authenticity is enhanced.

A private permissioned network powered by STACS Blockchain technology (Enhanced Ethereum) is known as the STACS Blockchain Platform. Despite continuing to use the Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) as the basis for the STACS Blockchain, there have been several improvements made to the core layers of the STACS Blockchain that have been implemented. As part of this platform, there is an Application Layer, consisting of a front-end Graphical User Interface (GUI) component connected to the underlying STACS Blockchain, and a Backend Application component connecting to the platform itself. It has been deployed on a variety of platforms since the platform-neutral deployment architecture was first deployed in 2019. These platforms include Dell on-premises infrastructure, Amazon Web Services (AWS), and Microsoft Azure private cloud.

It is implemented through a Defense in Depth strategy, which includes the front-end user interface, the Application Programming Interface (API) layer, and the blockchain setup to ensure cyber security is properly implemented. The implementation of multi-factor authentication is one of the methods used to protect the front-end user interface from being accessed by unauthorized users. To ensure that messages are secure in transit and to protect against attacks like man-in-the-middle attacks, the TLS protocol is used at the API layer. To safeguard against replay attacks, timestamps are also necessary for each API call to be performed. There is a process of “hardening” the blockchain nodes to prevent node-to-node communication between them by closing all unused network ports on the nodes. To prevent any hardware access to blockchain data, the blockchain data is encrypted at rest when it is stored in persistent storage.

Using a DLT infrastructure based on open-architecture, Project Benja intends to deploy a “Bond in a Box” platform that satisfies a demand among capital market participants and makes the deployment of an open-architecture platform uniquely possible. It is Bond in a Box's operating model that allows the platform to provide a greater number of services with fewer resources, reducing the time to market and improving cost and process efficiencies by providing more services with fewer resources. The use of a non-middleman platform, which investment banks and custodians can use to implement an end-to-end integrated issuer-to-investor servicing model, shows it to be cost-effective to implement. The indicative bond pricing is being compiled simultaneously on the STACS blockchain as part of the book-building process. It is no longer necessary to reconcile ledger data and conduct checks as a result of shared ledger data being widely accessible. As an additional benefit, blockchain technology and smart contracts have the advantage of eliminating the need to re-run multiple reconciliation processes and enabling straight-through processing as a result. Besides fulfilling legal and notary requirements, the STACS DLT serves as a general-purpose ledger and the Central Securities Depository features value-added functions in addition to its function as a general-purpose ledger.

In comparison, STACS has estimated that the “to-be” infrastructure setup proposed by Project Benja has led to up to a 75% reduction in the number of processes across origination, servicing, and post-trade and custody operations, which will lead to greater efficiencies. A parallel process of indicative bond pricing and flex takes place on the STACS blockchain where bond profiles, selling criteria, and other relevant information are prepared. Instead of soft-sounding discussions between lead and co-lead arrangers on indicative bond pricing and interests on the bond structuring leg, the process takes place concurrently on the STACS blockchain. Due to this, bond pricing and structuring will become more transparent and coordinated, and the valuations of every bond that is issued will be accurate and up to date for every bond issued as a result.

##  7 Project Genesis

During Project Genesis 1.0, the HKMA and the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) partnered with private consortia to address the inefficiencies in government green bond issuance, the uncertainty regarding the green impact promised at issuance, and the lack of liquid and transparent secondary markets for retail investors.

The intent of Project Genesis 2.0 was to address the issue of greenwashing of green bonds as an extension of Project Genesis 1.0’s successful proof of concept on the tokenization of retail green bonds using public and permissioned blockchains. In accordance with the Paris Agreement, a Mitigation Outcome Interest (MOI) is appended to a green bond with a commitment to deliver verified carbon credits upon maturity. A MOI is recognized by a national, international, or other recognized verification mechanism. Through the integration of the green bond and carbon markets, the carbon market is transformed from an ex-post reward to an ex-ante enabler for green projects.

As part of Project Genesis 2.0, blockchain, smart contracts, and IoT are explored as a means of tracking and recording real-time mitigation outcome data related to a digital MOI linked to a bond lifecycle in an immutable form that can be used to settle delivery obligations under the MOI. The purpose of this is to improve the real-time transparency of the environmental outcome of the asset or activities funded by the bond proceeds. Through the development of two prototypes for this project, investors will be able to track and trace back the environmental impact of the funded assets or activities in a timely and cost-effective manner, unlike the existing processes for measuring, reporting, and verifying carbon credits, which are time-consuming and manual. This provides investors with greater insight into the probability of receiving every Mitigation Outcome Unit (MOU), which allows them to manage the risks associated with any potential drawbacks associated with MOUs more effectively.

In collaboration with Digital Asset, Goldman Sachs (Asia) LLC, and Allinfra, a prototype solution has been developed for Project Genesis 2.0, offering a simulated solution for the digital tracking, delivery, and transfer of MOIs (later settled through the delivery of MOUs), and tokenizing the issuance of the green bond to create a digital end-to-end financial system for institutional green debt. This solution incorporates IoT technology, blockchain technology, and smart contracts.

Using a blockchain-based platform, the consortium demonstrated a straight-through process for creating, transferring, and redeeming MOIs. A key objective of this project was to develop a scalable prototype that could respond instantly to any given state of digital assets (i.e., retired, pending, active) and can be employed to introduce new asset types quickly and effectively. To minimize errors and operational burdens, workflows have been streamlined to reduce error rates. Other benefits include access to the market and the ability to source liquidity in addition to visibility into an asset's provenance. By synchronizing interstate processes and issuing assets in real time, issuers can monetize their ESG assets. Consequently, better cash flows are supported, and financing gaps are filled.

Using the Defense Against Money Laundering (DAML) smart contract technology, the DAP ESG prototype, illustrated in [Fig. 6](#Ch022_321-333_B978044334717700009X.xhtml#f0035) above \[20\], streamlines the ESG finance value chain by utilizing blockchain, DLT, and IoT. In Project Genesis 2.0, Hyperledger Besu network capabilities are employed in conjunction with the privacy-enabled Canton blockchain from Digital Asset. It provides secure synchronization among multiple nodes on a variety of platforms and manages the progression of all workflows in the solution.

![Fig. 6 DAP ESG prototype technical architecture.](images/B978044334717700009X/f22-06-9780443347177.jpg)

[Fig. 6](#Ch022_321-333_B978044334717700009X.xhtml#B-f0035) DAP ESG prototype technical architecture.

The diagram illustrates the Goldman Sachs Blockchain Integration Platform E S G Prototype. At the top, I o T Devices on Asset Source connect to the Allinfra Platform, which includes Allinfra Climate and Asset Registry. Below this, the Goldman Sachs Prototype UI and Goldman Sachs Blockchain Integration Platform E S G Prototype are shown. The Daml Smart Contracts section includes Digital Debt Securities, MO I & M O U and various tokenization models, services and workflows such as Origination, Book Building, Issuance, Trading, Settlement, Custody and Lifecycle slash Corp Actions. The D L T section includes L 2 Canton with D a m l Part icipant Nodes and L 1 Blockchain with Enterprise Blockchain Nodes. Consortium D L T slash Blockchains are connected to D a m l drivers. On the right, there are sections for Carbon Marketplaces, N D C Registries, Digital Cash Networks (on public slash private D L T) and Other Asset Chains slash Platforms (public slash private D L T).

The data related to carbon emissions is collected directly from asset devices by Allinfra Climate, and the data is stored permanently in an API that can be used for a variety of reporting and verification needs. It is important to ensure that the operational data related to carbon is recorded in a way that ensures a consistent and permanent link between the data that supports environmental financial products and the data source, which is normally necessary for the measurement and verification of emission reductions. As an additional source of contextual information, additional data can be ingested from other on-site and off-site devices that can measure the output of the energy source (for example, pyrometer data for solar, or anemometer data for wind, both of which can measure the power output of the energy source).

Goldman Sachs’ ESG prototype of the blockchain platform offers flexible and reliable integration services between on-chain processes, ledger transactions, and other conventional systems. An API integration with Allinfra Climate was implemented during the simulation process to ensure that asset data was updated in a timely manner as well as to determine the number of MOUs that were generated as accurately as possible. While a limited number of deployment options were available for the simulation, participants (such as syndicate banks, brokers, dealers, ESG auditors, custodians, and investors) theoretically have three different ways to interact with the platform and the underlying network, each with varying levels of technical integration and trust. GUI/API connectivity is the first step, followed by the hosting of DAML participant nodes, and finally, the installation of full DLT and node hosting for DAML participants is the final step.

Investor 1 acts by using a participant node hosted by a syndicate bank (the “Syndicate Bank Participant Node”) and GUI/API. Investor 1 authorizes the Syndicate Bank Participant Node to fill out and sign smart contracts before sending the completed documents to the underlying ledger for verification. In addition to the counterparty and custodian of Investor 1’s transaction, other nodes in the Syndicate Bank Participant Node confirm the legitimacy of the DAML contract contained in the transaction. In a similar manner to Investor 1, Investor 2 is also accessing the DLT through a third-party participant node.

It is possible for participants to submit contracts signed with their own private keys by hosting their own DAML participant node. The participants can opt to host their own DAML participant node and DLT node to execute smart contracts as well as send and sign transactions to the underlying ledger using their identities. Using this model, network access is uninterrupted, complete cryptographic security is provided, and verifiability is assured.

##  8 Discussion

Consensus algorithm is a major factor that determines the blockchain's throughput, scalability, and performance. It is also a major technical consideration when integrating blockchain with IoT. Common consensuses like Proof of Work (PoW) or Proof of Stake (PoS) are not effective for IoT due to latency, while the high energy consumption for PoW is a major ESG concern. Transaction processing is accelerated and made more effective by Solana Labs’ Proof of History (PoH). It accomplishes this by using a series of hashes that are cryptographically secure and verifiable to arrange transactions and blocks in a Blockchain network. To do this, PoH creates a timestamp for every block in the Blockchain using a cryptographic Verifiable Delay Function (VDF). However, because PoH also calls for additional computational resources, it might have a large energy footprint.

In fact, STACS's blockchain adopts a blended use of Reliable, Replicated, Redundant and Fault Tolerant (RAFT) and Byzantine Fault Tolerant (BFT) for its consensus. RAFT ensures that only one transaction is created at any point in time for transaction finality, while BFT synchronizes blockchain state across the network and prevents double spending. This approach is optimized for transaction speed and energy consumption. IOTA's Tangle protocol ([www.iota.org](http://www.iota.org)) is another potential solution for this challenge. Based on Direct Acyclic Graph (DAG) consensus, Tangle also consumes a low level of energy while delivering high scalability and throughputs at zero fee. However, Tangle relies on a centralized party called “The Coordinator” to confirm transactions, which essentially removes the trustless quality of blockchain technology.

It is also worth noting that blockchain solution may not be the optimal choice for every process in the whole ESG data journey. For example, for data aggregators and orchestrators in Project Greenprint, API connections can be leveraged to provide secured access for other stakeholders, without sacrificing the high performance which is not a strength of blockchain technology.

It is imperative that oracles are used when working with smart contracts to provide real-world data that can be trusted. IoT unreliability may have an adverse effect on the verification of these smart contracts. Furthermore, smart contracts could be overloaded with access to several data sources. While smart contracts are currently distributed and decentralized, they do not share resources to allocate tasks or handle large amounts of computation. Therefore, while there is only one node for executing smart contracts, multiple nodes are involved in executing the code. Consequently, IoT must rely on the distributed capabilities of cloud computing and big data to increase its processing power.

A smart contract should also consider the variability and limitations associated with the IoT. To ensure that apps can handle the IoT based on the situation and requirements, smart contracts should be utilized in conjunction with filtering and grouping techniques. An instantaneous device integration method may make these applications even more powerful. Furthermore, IoT responses would be quicker as a result of smart contract actuation mechanisms.

There is a great challenge now when it comes to creating distributed applications that span multiple organizations with today's technology. All organizations must concur on data encoding, transport protocols, and interaction guidelines for each application. They must also correctly implement their respective parts of the interaction, such as authentication and authorization. Once implemented, these applications frequently become isolated silos because there is no universally useful, safe, and privacy-preserving way to integrate them and create the business workflows they automate. To break down these silos, smart contract platforms like Ethereum face scalability, authorization, and privacy issues. Platforms like Ethereum's scaling issues and concerns about privacy are both resolved by the DAML interoperability protocol. It makes it possible for developers to strike a balance between the need for auditability and data privacy, which makes it ideal for creating GDPR-compliant systems. Depending on the need for trust, different synchronization domain implementation strategies can be used in the protocol. Domains can be launched whenever there are scalability, operational, or trust issues. They require specific permissions but can be federated at no extra cost for interoperability, creating a virtual global ledger that makes it possible to compose business workflows that are truly global in scope.

##  9 Summary

There is a rapidly emerging mission across a wide range of disciplines to create a data platform and encourage ESG finance to achieve a sustainable future and foster a green economy. To ultimately achieve the goal of aligning investments with their ESG mandates, investors and issuers alike can have a transparent and timely view of their portfolio holdings by utilizing blockchain-based platforms, as demonstrated in Project Greenprint, Project Benja, and Project Genesis 2.0. Our study provides a comprehensive view of how blockchain technology and IoT could be incorporated into the design and enhancement of such platforms, as a result of which we provide an overall illustration. Since these two digital technologies are relatively new and are improving very rapidly, further work will be required to overcome their current technical challenges.
